taxonomy.title: Stomach — adenocarcinoma, GIST and lymphoma
taxonomy.scopeIn: Gastric adenocarcinoma staging and resection, gastric GIST diagnosis and treatment, gastric lymphoma and organ-specific tissue adequacy.
taxonomy.scopeOut: General cancer biology and germline principles belong to oncology-genetics-principles. Benign gastric disease belongs to stomach-ulcer-bleeding-motility.

concepts.displayName: Avoid routine prophylactic splenectomy in proximal gastric cancer
concepts.learningObjective: Preserve the spleen during curative gastrectomy for proximal gastric adenocarcinoma when there is no greater-curvature invasion, direct splenic invasion, or suspected splenic-hilar disease.
concepts.assignmentBasis: Organ/decision-family assignment reviewed against the topic scope.

concepts.displayName: EUS core and molecular evaluation of selected gastric GIST
concepts.learningObjective: Select EUS-guided core tissue and molecular testing when a challenging gastric mass may receive preoperative targeted therapy.
concepts.assignmentBasis: Organ/decision-family assignment reviewed against the topic scope.

concepts.displayName: Mutation-guided neoadjuvant planning for challenging GIST
concepts.learningObjective: Select neoadjuvant imatinib only for an imatinib-sensitive GIST when shrinkage is expected to reduce operative morbidity.
concepts.assignmentBasis: Organ/decision-family assignment reviewed against the topic scope.

concepts.displayName: H. pylori eradication as initial treatment for localized gastric MALT lymphoma
concepts.learningObjective: Select H. pylori eradication as initial treatment for the classic localized low-grade presentation and preserve confirmation and response-reassessment boundaries.
concepts.assignmentBasis: Organ/decision-family assignment reviewed against the topic scope.

concepts.displayName: Choose gastric MALT care from post-eradication trajectory
concepts.learningObjective: Distinguish regressing asymptomatic residual gastric MALT or molecular persistence from progressive symptomatic disease after interpretable infection reassessment, and choose monitoring versus escalation.
concepts.assignmentBasis: Organ/decision-family assignment reviewed against the topic scope.

concepts.displayName: Pathologic recognition of gastric MALT lymphoma
concepts.learningObjective: Recognize gastric MALT lymphoma from integrated small B-cell morphology, lymphoepithelial lesions, and compatible immunophenotyping while avoiding diagnosis from CD20 alone.
concepts.assignmentBasis: Organ/decision-family assignment reviewed against the topic scope.

concepts.displayName: Apply gastric lymphoma morphology to the treatment pathway
concepts.learningObjective: Integrate gastric small-cell architecture, molecular-test limitations and the actual distribution of large cells before selecting an indolent MALT rather than aggressive/reactive care pathway.
concepts.assignmentBasis: Organ/decision-family assignment reviewed against the topic scope.

concepts.displayName: Gastric cancer with adjacent-organ invasion
concepts.learningObjective: Distinguish a routine prophylactic organ removal from specialist assessment of direct adjacent-organ invasion during gastric cancer resection planning.
concepts.assignmentBasis: Organ/decision-family assignment reviewed against the topic scope.

concepts.displayName: Gastric cancer with adjacent-organ invasion
concepts.learningObjective: Use organ-specific operative interfaces to distinguish indicated splenic extension from prophylactic pancreatic resection during gastric cancer surgery.
concepts.assignmentBasis: Organ/decision-family assignment reviewed against the topic scope.

concepts.displayName: Gastric cancer with adjacent-organ invasion
concepts.learningObjective: Use organ-specific operative interfaces to distinguish indicated splenic extension from prophylactic pancreatic resection during gastric cancer surgery.
concepts.assignmentBasis: Organ/decision-family assignment reviewed against the topic scope.

concepts.displayName: A mucosal specimen does not classify an unsampled wall mass
concepts.learningObjective: Assess whether the submitted gastric specimen represents the wall lesion before using it to clear or initiate targeted tumor treatment.
concepts.assignmentBasis: Organ/decision-family assignment reviewed against the topic scope.

concepts.displayName: Changed gastric lymphoma tissue
concepts.learningObjective: Recognize a new aggressive tissue pattern after an eradication response as a reason to reassess the lymphoma pathway rather than repeat infection-directed treatment.
concepts.assignmentBasis: Organ/decision-family assignment reviewed against the topic scope.

concepts.displayName: Changed gastric lymphoma tissue
concepts.learningObjective: Resolve uncertain gastric lymphoma classification before selecting restaging and treatment for apparent progression.
concepts.assignmentBasis: Organ/decision-family assignment reviewed against the topic scope.

question.stem: Which diagnostic plan should be arranged next for {patientName}'s gastric mass?

answerChoices.label: EUS core biopsy with molecular testing
EUS-guided fine-needle aspiration cytology
answerChoices.distractorRationale: Cytology alone may not provide the histologic and molecular material needed for this plan.

answerChoices.label: PET-CT without tissue sampling
answerChoices.distractorRationale: Metabolic imaging does not provide the tissue diagnosis and genotype required here.

answerChoices.label: Percutaneous core biopsy of the mass
answerChoices.distractorRationale: A percutaneous route is not preferred when EUS can obtain the needed tissue while limiting spill risk.

question.stem: Which operative plan should be discussed for {patientName}?

answerChoices.label: Gastrectomy with D2 lymphadenectomy and spleen preservation
answerChoices.rationale: Integrates the wall-depth finding with nodal extent while avoiding routine removal of an uninvolved spleen.

answerChoices.label: Gastrectomy with D1 lymphadenectomy and spleen preservation
answerChoices.distractorRationale: Preserves the organ but underestimates the nodal extent appropriate to the represented invasive stage.

answerChoices.label: Gastrectomy with D2 lymphadenectomy and splenic resection
answerChoices.distractorRationale: Provides the nodal extent but adds prophylactic organ removal without a supplied therapeutic indication.

answerChoices.label: Gastrectomy with D1 lymphadenectomy and splenic resection
answerChoices.distractorRationale: Combines an inadequate nodal extent for the represented stage with unindicated splenic removal.

question.explanation: The wall-depth observation supports an invasive stage requiring appropriate D2 nodal planning in an experienced service. That does not require routine splenectomy in the represented anatomy. This item does not resolve the separately documented JGCA English splenic-hilar wording discrepancy or prescribe a disputed station-10 rule.

question.stem: Which area should be prioritized as evidence for {patientName}'s subtype classification?

answerChoices.label: Area B for integrated subtype assessment
answerChoices.rationale: The small-cell gland-infiltrating and epithelial-disrupting pattern contributes relevant architecture to the known lineage/clonality findings. It does not make a single feature universally necessary or sufficient for the subtype.

answerChoices.label: Area A for integrated subtype assessment
answerChoices.distractorRationale: A polarized macrophage-rich follicle is conspicuous but does not supply the same small-cell gland relationship. The known B-cell clone does not make every lymphoid area equally specific.

answerChoices.label: Area C for integrated subtype assessment
answerChoices.distractorRationale: Scattered large cells warrant attention but are not the same as a diffuse large-cell component. Their presence alone does not replace the relevant small-cell architectural assessment.

question.explanation: Lineage and clonality require morphological context. Among these constructed fields, the gland-infiltrating small-cell pattern provides the most relevant additional architecture for integrated MALT assessment. A prominent follicle and scattered large cells require interpretation rather than automatic subtype labels; none of these observations alone closes the diagnosis.

question.stem: Which patient best fits initial treatment with H. pylori eradication?

answerChoices.label: Localized H. pylori-positive low-grade gastric MALT without transformation
Gastric diffuse large B-cell lymphoma with sheets of transformed large cells
answerChoices.distractorRationale: This is an aggressive transformed histology and does not fit the approved classic low-grade eradication-first concept.

answerChoices.label: Localized gastric MALT that progressed after confirmed H. pylori eradication
answerChoices.distractorRationale: Progression after an adequate eradication pathway requires reassessment and a different treatment decision.

answerChoices.label: Disseminated symptomatic gastric MALT with threatened organ function
answerChoices.distractorRationale: Threatening or advanced symptomatic disease requires specialist reassessment rather than an eradication-only strategy.

question.explanation: The approved eradication-first teaching point applies to localized low-grade H. pylori-positive gastric MALT without transformation or threatening disease.

question.stem: Which interpretation and initial-care plan should be discussed with {patientName}?

answerChoices.label: Gastric MALT lymphoma: eradication and histologic review
answerChoices.rationale: The fusion is not present in all MALT lymphoma. Negative FISH does not overturn compatible integrated morphology or remove the need for response assessment.

answerChoices.label: Reactive gastritis: infection care and clinical review
answerChoices.distractorRationale: A negative subtype-associated molecular test is not a sensitive exclusion test for MALT lymphoma.

answerChoices.label: Indeterminate infiltrate: repeat fusion testing before treatment
answerChoices.distractorRationale: Repeating the same negative molecular result does not resolve or override the already available integrated tissue findings.

decisionNodes.currentUpdate: After completed eradication, the urea breath test is negative six weeks after treatment started and two weeks after stopping proton-pump inhibitors. Serial endoscopy shows the gastric ulcer enlarging rather than healing, and recurrent bleeding has lowered hemoglobin. Repeat mapped biopsies show increasing low-grade MALT infiltration. Restaging still confines the disease to the stomach; there is no confluent large-cell component.

answerChoices.label: Involved-site radiotherapy with histologic review
answerChoices.rationale: Localized symptomatic, overtly progressive disease after infection clearance warrants escalation rather than monitoring a regressing residual pattern.

answerChoices.rationale: Observation of asymptomatic residual disease does not apply unchanged to worsening ulceration, bleeding and increasing infiltration.

case.learningSummary: Molecular tests have different roles from integrated diagnosis. BIRC3-MALT1 is not detected in every gastric MALT lymphoma, so its absence cannot exclude an otherwise supported classification. Use the morphology and clinical extent to plan eradication-led care and histologic response review. Slow histologic clearance and overt progression are different clinical states. Localized gastric MALT with symptomatic or adverse progression after eradication should be assessed for involved-site radiotherapy. Do not infer persistent infection from residual lymphoma or apply watchful monitoring without considering the actual trajectory.

items.label: Original biopsy
items.value: Small B cells with gland-infiltrating lymphoepithelial lesions and a compatible MALT immunophenotype.

items.label: Current endoscopy
items.value: A new raised ulcerated focus at a different gastric site.

items.label: Current specimen
items.value: Two tiny crushed fragments. Large atypical B cells are present, but their architecture and proportion cannot be established from the submitted material.

items.label: Outside summary
items.value: Relapsed gastric MALT lymphoma; radiation discussion requested.

items.label: Current symptoms
items.value: New early satiety and weight loss without bleeding or obstruction.

answerChoices.rationale: The new material does not securely classify the changed lesion. More diagnostic tissue is needed before treating it as the same low-grade process or selecting a staging pathway for a different one.

answerChoices.rationale: This could contribute to staging a classified local lymphoma, but depth information does not resolve the changed lesion's uncertain histology.

question.explanation: The outside label exceeds what the small crushed sample establishes. New large atypical cells in a changed lesion require adequate tissue classification before the next lymphoma plan. question.patientPresentation: A patient with resectable proximal gastric adenocarcinoma otherwise meets the criteria for spleen-preserving gastrectomy.
question.stem: Which new finding makes the routine spleen-preservation rule less directly applicable?

answerChoices.label: Direct extension of the tumor into the spleen
Location of the tumor in the proximal stomach
answerChoices.distractorRationale: Proximal location is part of the approved scenario and does not alone justify splenectomy.

answerChoices.label: A planned total gastrectomy for oncologic resection
answerChoices.distractorRationale: Total gastrectomy alone does not make prophylactic splenectomy beneficial.

answerChoices.label: Need for standard regional lymph-node staging
answerChoices.distractorRationale: Standard regional nodal staging does not by itself require removal of the spleen.

question.explanation: Direct splenic invasion is outside the routine prophylactic setting. This boundary does not independently prescribe an operation; it signals that individualized oncologic planning is required.

question.patientPresentation: The hospital surgical team is reviewing several patients with proximal gastric adenocarcinoma before definitive operative planning.
question.stem: Which patient most clearly fits the evidence supporting routine spleen preservation?

answerChoices.label: Proximal cancer without greater-curvature, splenic, or hilar involvement
Proximal cancer with direct tumor invasion extending into splenic parenchyma
answerChoices.distractorRationale: Direct splenic invasion falls outside the routine prophylactic-splenectomy evidence addressed by this concept.

answerChoices.label: Proximal cancer with suspected metastatic disease in splenic-hilar nodes
answerChoices.distractorRationale: Suspected splenic-hilar disease falls outside the narrowly approved routine spleen-preservation population.

answerChoices.label: Proximal cancer with extensive tumor invasion along the greater curvature
answerChoices.distractorRationale: Greater-curvature invasion was excluded from the pivotal routine-prophylaxis population and requires separate operative planning.

question.explanation: The strongest routine spleen-preservation evidence applies when proximal gastric cancer does not involve the greater curvature, spleen, or splenic-hilar nodes.

question.patientPresentation: A patient has resectable proximal gastric adenocarcinoma. Staging shows no greater-curvature extension, splenic invasion, or suspicious splenic-hilar nodes. Curative gastrectomy is planned.
question.stem: What should the operative referral recommend regarding the spleen?

answerChoices.label: Add splenectomy to every total gastrectomy
answerChoices.distractorRationale: A planned total gastrectomy is not by itself an indication for prophylactic splenectomy.

answerChoices.label: Avoid routine prophylactic splenectomy
Add splenectomy for proximal location alone
answerChoices.distractorRationale: Proximal location alone does not justify routine splenic removal in the approved population.

answerChoices.label: Add splenectomy solely to increase node yield
answerChoices.distractorRationale: Increasing node yield alone does not provide a survival justification for prophylactic splenectomy.

question.explanation: In proximal gastric adenocarcinoma without greater-curvature invasion, direct splenic invasion, or suspected splenic-hilar disease, routine prophylactic splenectomy adds morbidity without improving survival.

question.stem: Which next investigation should clarify {patientName}'s gastric infiltrate?

answerChoices.label: Repeat endoscopy with documented-site biopsies for histologic comparison
answerChoices.rationale: Resolves integrated diagnostic uncertainty instead of treating a clone plus lineage as established MALT lymphoma.

answerChoices.label: BIRC3-MALT1 fusion testing on the recorded gastric biopsy material
answerChoices.distractorRationale: Is useful in established gastric MALT evaluation but does not alone resolve the current morphologic classification.

answerChoices.label: Repeat immunoglobulin gene-rearrangement analysis on a second DNA extraction
answerChoices.distractorRationale: Can corroborate a clone but does not convert clonality without characteristic morphology into a lymphoma diagnosis.

question.explanation: B-cell lineage and a clonal rearrangement need morphologic/clinical correlation: chronic inflammation can contain clonal B-cell expansions. The preserved gland epithelium in this sampled infiltrate does not supply the characteristic destructive gland interaction. Repeat documented biopsies and comparative expert review are appropriate for diagnostic uncertainty. Fusion testing and repeat clonality can contribute, but do not replace that assessment.

answerChoices.rationale: Resolves integrated diagnostic uncertainty instead of treating a clone plus lineage as established MALT lymphoma.

answerChoices.label: BIRC3-MALT1 fusion testing on the recorded gastric biopsy material
answerChoices.rationale: Is useful in established gastric MALT evaluation but does not alone resolve the current morphologic classification.

answerChoices.label: Repeat immunoglobulin gene-rearrangement analysis on a second DNA extraction
answerChoices.rationale: Can corroborate a clone but does not convert clonality without characteristic morphology into a lymphoma diagnosis.

decisionNodes.explanation: B-cell lineage and a clonal rearrangement need morphologic/clinical correlation: chronic inflammation can contain clonal B-cell expansions. The preserved gland epithelium in this sampled infiltrate does not supply the characteristic destructive gland interaction. Repeat documented biopsies and comparative expert review are appropriate for diagnostic uncertainty. Fusion testing and repeat clonality can contribute, but do not replace that assessment.

question.stem: Which interpretation should guide {patientName}'s next care?

answerChoices.label: Keep the classification open and obtain correlated histologic assessment
answerChoices.rationale: Clonality and B-cell lineage do not settle a morphologically unresolved infiltrate; retain diagnostic review rather than assign a definitive lymphoma or reactive category.

answerChoices.label: Assign gastric MALT lymphoma and enter its treatment pathway
answerChoices.distractorRationale: A clonal population may occur with chronic inflammation; the stated evidence does not independently establish the lymphoma classification.

answerChoices.label: Assign reactive gastritis and end the lymphoma assessment
answerChoices.distractorRationale: Preserved glands in these sections do not by themselves exclude all MALT lymphoma or make this limited distribution definitive.

question.explanation: A clonal B-cell result is interpreted with morphology and clinical context. It neither independently establishes gastric MALT lymphoma nor makes preserved glands proof of benignity. The correct decision here is to retain diagnostic assessment. This question deliberately does not rank fusion testing, deeper sections and repeat endoscopy as interchangeable next investigations.

question.stem: Which conclusion and histology-review goal are supported by {patientName}'s current findings?

answerChoices.label: Clonal B-cell infiltrate; assess cytology and architecture
answerChoices.rationale: The clone is demonstrated, but lineage/clonality alone do not establish MALT lymphoma from the limited architecture shown.

answerChoices.label: Clonal B-cell infiltrate, MALT type; assess large-cell component
answerChoices.distractorRationale: This assigns the specific lymphoma diagnosis before its morphological basis is established; preserved glands do not themselves prove or exclude it.

answerChoices.label: Clonal B-cell infiltrate, reactive type; assess Helicobacter activity
answerChoices.distractorRationale: The limited preserved-gland sample does not establish reactive status merely because classic destructive architecture is not shown.

question.explanation: A demonstrated B-cell clone is an evidence finding, not automatically a specific lymphoma diagnosis. Morphological review must assess the infiltrate's cytology and architecture in context. Preserved epithelium in this limited site neither excludes MALT nor establishes reactive gastritis. This does not uniquely rank repeat endoscopy, further sections and molecular studies for every such case.

question.stem: Which area should be prioritized as evidence for {patientName}'s subtype classification?

answerChoices.label: Area B for integrated subtype assessment
answerChoices.rationale: Small B-cell morphology together with gland-infiltrating epithelial disruption contributes the architecture that a clone alone cannot supply. It supports integrated MALT assessment without making one feature universally required or sufficient.

answerChoices.label: Area A for integrated subtype assessment
answerChoices.distractorRationale: A conspicuous follicle and its polarized, macrophage-rich pattern can attract attention, but those features alone do not provide the gland-infiltrating small-cell evidence in the other area.

answerChoices.label: Area C for integrated subtype assessment
answerChoices.distractorRationale: Large cells can attract concern for transformation, but scattered large cells among smaller lymphocytes do not themselves establish a diffuse large-cell component. The offered focal pattern does not replace integrated subtype morphology.

question.explanation: The deeper levels change the available morphology. Small B cells entering and disrupting gland epithelium provide relevant architecture alongside the clonal lineage finding. A prominent polarized follicle or scattered large cells must also be reviewed, but neither by itself establishes the subtype or a transformed large-cell process. Classification remains an integrated hematopathology judgment; lymphoepithelial lesions are not asserted to be universally necessary.

question.stem: Which diagnosis best fits the integrated biopsy findings?

answerChoices.label: Gastric MALT lymphoma
Diffuse large B-cell lymphoma involving the stomach
answerChoices.distractorRationale: DLBCL is characterized by sheets of transformed large B cells, which are absent in this approved presentation.

answerChoices.label: Gastric adenocarcinoma with reactive lymphoid inflammation
answerChoices.distractorRationale: The biopsy describes a clonal-appearing small B-cell process with lymphoepithelial lesions rather than malignant epithelial cells.

answerChoices.label: Mantle cell lymphoma involving the gastric mucosa
answerChoices.distractorRationale: Mantle cell lymphoma commonly expresses CD5 and cyclin D1, unlike the approved immunophenotype.

question.explanation: Small B cells infiltrating gastric glands to form lymphoepithelial lesions, with CD20 and CD79a expression and absent CD5, CD10, and cyclin D1, support gastric MALT lymphoma. The morphology and immunophenotype must be interpreted together.

question.stem: What is the most appropriate initial lymphoma-directed plan?

answerChoices.label: H. pylori eradication therapy, then response reassessment
Immediate gastrectomy followed by routine postoperative surveillance
answerChoices.distractorRationale: Gastrectomy is not the preferred initial treatment for this classic localized low-grade eradication-responsive presentation.

answerChoices.label: Immediate R-CHOP before attempting H. pylori eradication therapy
answerChoices.distractorRationale: Aggressive systemic lymphoma treatment is not the initial approach for this low-grade nontransformed presentation.

answerChoices.label: Definitive gastric radiotherapy without an initial eradication attempt
answerChoices.distractorRationale: The approved classic H. pylori-positive localized presentation should first receive eradication therapy.

question.explanation: H. pylori eradication is initial lymphoma-directed treatment for this classic localized low-grade presentation. Eradication must be confirmed and lymphoma response reassessed; this is not permission to omit follow-up.

decisionNodes.stem: Which diagnosis best fits {patientName}'s integrated biopsy findings?

answerChoices.label: Gastric extranodal marginal-zone lymphoma
answerChoices.rationale: Integrates the gland-infiltrating marginal-zone-type architecture and typical B-cell marker profile.

answerChoices.label: Gastric follicular lymphoma
answerChoices.rationale: Requires a different integrated architectural/germinal-center pattern rather than B-cell lineage alone.

answerChoices.label: Gastric mantle-cell lymphoma
answerChoices.rationale: Is a small-B-cell competitor but is not favored by the integrated marker/architectural findings.

decisionNodes.explanation: The architecture and phenotype together support MALT-type extranodal marginal-zone lymphoma. decisionNodes.currentUpdate: The gastric infiltrate contains small atypical B cells with irregular nuclei and pale cytoplasm expanding the lamina propria and entering gland epithelium. CD20 and CD79a stain the infiltrate; CD5, CD10 and cyclin D1 do not.
decisionNodes.stem: Which diagnosis fits {patientName}'s integrated gastric biopsy findings?

answerChoices.label: Gastric extranodal marginal-zone lymphoma
answerChoices.rationale: Integrates the gland-infiltrating marginal-zone-type architecture and typical B-cell marker profile.

answerChoices.label: Gastric follicular lymphoma
answerChoices.rationale: Requires a different integrated architectural/germinal-center pattern rather than B-cell lineage alone.

answerChoices.label: Gastric mantle-cell lymphoma
answerChoices.rationale: Is a small-B-cell competitor but is not favored by the integrated marker/architectural findings.

decisionNodes.explanation: The architecture and phenotype together support MALT-type extranodal marginal-zone lymphoma. Follicular and mantle-cell lymphoma are closer small-B-cell alternatives than a large-cell label dismissed by a size adjective. Marker exceptions still require integrated pathology review.

case.learningSummary:
Small B cells infiltrating gastric glands to form lymphoepithelial lesions, with CD20 and CD79a expression and absent CD5, CD10, and cyclin D1, support gastric MALT lymphoma. The morphology and immunophenotype must be interpreted together.

H. pylori eradication is initial lymphoma-directed treatment for this classic localized low-grade presentation. Eradication must be confirmed and lymphoma response reassessed; this is not permission to omit follow-up.

question.patientPresentation: An adult with localized H. pylori-positive low-grade gastric MALT is preparing to begin eradication therapy and asks what happens after the medication course.
question.stem: Which explanation best describes the treatment pathway?

answerChoices.label: Eradicate H. pylori first, then reassess the lymphoma response
Because CD20 is positive, begin rituximab before addressing H. pylori
answerChoices.distractorRationale: CD20 expression does not displace eradication as the initial strategy for this approved presentation.

answerChoices.label: Any CD20-positive gastric lymphoma can be treated with eradication alone
answerChoices.distractorRationale: CD20 is not disease-specific, and aggressive or nonclassic gastric lymphomas require different management.

answerChoices.label: Gastrectomy is required before response can be assessed endoscopically
answerChoices.distractorRationale: Endoscopic biopsy reassessment follows eradication; routine gastrectomy is not required for this pathway.

question.explanation: Eradication is the initial lymphoma treatment, not the end of care. Confirm eradication and reassess the gastric lymphoma endoscopically and histologically, recognizing that regression may be delayed.

answerChoices.rationale: Treats the infection-linked localized lymphoma and retains assessment of the lymphoma response rather than equating the medication course with completed care.

answerChoices.rationale: Overweights the B-cell marker and replaces the indicated initial infection-directed approach and gastric tissue reassessment.

answerChoices.rationale: Treats clinical improvement or completion of medication as an adequate substitute for assessing the lymphoma response.

case.learningSummary:
The combination of small B-cell morphology, lymphoepithelial lesions, and a CD20-positive, CD5-negative, CD10-negative, cyclin D1-negative phenotype supports gastric MALT lymphoma.

Eradication is the initial lymphoma treatment, not the end of care. Confirm eradication and reassess the gastric lymphoma endoscopically and histologically, recognizing that regression may be delayed.

node.currentUpdate: Atypical B cells expand the gastric lamina propria and infiltrate glands. CD20 and CD79a stain the infiltrate; CD5, CD10 and cyclin D1 do not. The specimen does not show sheets of transformed large cells.

answerChoices.rationale: Is a closer small-B-cell alternative, but the supplied architecture and absent germinal-center marker do not favor it.

question.stem: Which operative planning step should be discussed for {patientName}'s documented adjacent-organ extension?

answerChoices.label: Specialist assessment for en-bloc multivisceral resection
answerChoices.rationale: Direct invasion changes the question from prophylactic organ removal to whether involved organs can be included in an appropriate curative operation.

answerChoices.label: Gastrectomy with mandatory pancreatic and splenic preservation
answerChoices.rationale: The no-prophylactic-resection rule does not require leaving directly invaded adjacent organs behind.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: The no-prophylactic-resection rule does not require leaving directly invaded adjacent organs behind.

answerChoices.label: Gastrectomy with routine splenectomy and pancreatic preservation
answerChoices.rationale: This substitutes an automatic organ rule for assessment of the actual two-organ extension.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: This substitutes an automatic organ rule for assessment of the actual two-organ extension.

question.explanation: Routine prophylactic splenectomy is different from evaluating direct invasion. The recorded evidence permits consideration of combined pancreatic and splenic resection for relevant invasion; it does not establish that this patient is automatically resectable or specify a treatment sequence.

question.stem: Which adjacent-organ plan should accompany {patientName}'s gastrectomy based on the recorded findings?
question.explanation: Interpret each organ interface separately. The splenic-hilar finding differs from a prophylactic splenectomy scenario; a separate pancreatic plane does not justify default pancreatic removal. This extent decision follows represented staging/feasibility review and is not a complete multimodality treatment recommendation.

answerChoices.label: Splenectomy and pancreatic preservation
answerChoices.rationale: The splenic-hilar finding takes this outside routine spleen-preservation scope, while the represented pancreatic plane does not establish a reason for pancreatic-tail removal.

answerChoices.label: Splenectomy and distal pancreatectomy
answerChoices.rationale: An initial concern for adjacent invasion should not automatically become removal of every nearby organ after a separable pancreatic interface is observed.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: An initial concern for adjacent invasion should not automatically become removal of every nearby organ after a separable pancreatic interface is observed.

answerChoices.label: Splenic preservation and pancreatic preservation
answerChoices.rationale: A general avoidance of prophylactic organ removal does not apply unchanged to the documented splenic-hilar involvement.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: A general avoidance of prophylactic organ removal does not apply unchanged to the documented splenic-hilar involvement.

answerChoices.label: Splenic preservation and distal pancreatectomy
answerChoices.rationale: This reverses the organ-specific observations, removing the separable pancreas while retaining the involved splenic-hilar target.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: This reverses the organ-specific observations, removing the separable pancreas while retaining the involved splenic-hilar target.

question.stem: Which operative plan best fits {patientName}'s recorded interface findings?
question.explanation: A smaller radiographic interface after treatment does not prove that previously represented direct invasion has become safe to peel apart. In the specified locally resectable setting, plan en-bloc removal rather than divide through the persistent bridge or infer unresectability from adjacency itself. This is a retrospective extent decision, not a claim that every adherent proximal gastric cancer requires multivisceral resection.

exhibit.caption: Constructed teaching record; fictional patient observations

items.label: Staging
items.value: No peritoneal deposits or other distant disease at operative assessment

items.label: Local anatomy
items.value: The firm bridge extends to the splenic hilum; proximal pancreatic division and gastric resection margins can be placed outside the bridge

answerChoices.label: En-bloc gastrectomy and distal pancreatectomy/splenectomy
answerChoices.rationale: Prior represented pancreatic invasion plus a persistent inseparable bridge makes peeling through that interface an oncologic compromise; the represented margins support an en-bloc local plan.

answerChoices.label: Gastrectomy after pancreatic-plane separation; retain spleen
answerChoices.rationale: A radiographic response does not establish that an inseparable previously invaded interface is safe to divide through.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: A radiographic response does not establish that an inseparable previously invaded interface is safe to divide through.

answerChoices.label: Palliative gastrojejunostomy with gastric tumor left in situ
answerChoices.rationale: This is credible when disease cannot be cleared or distant disease prevents the intended curative operation, neither of which follows from the recorded local bridge.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: This is credible when disease cannot be cleared or distant disease prevents the intended curative operation, neither of which follows from the recorded local bridge.

case.presentation: {patientName}, a 64-year-old man, reviews his gastrectomy record in clinic. Before systemic treatment, a biopsy taken through the gastric mass showed malignant glands within pancreatic tissue. Restaging later showed no distant disease and less soft-tissue thickening at that interface. At operation a firm bridge still joined stomach and pancreatic tail; the surgeon could not develop a plane through it.

question.stem: Which evidence plan is needed before {patientName}'s wall mass can enter a mutation-guided preoperative treatment pathway?

answerChoices.label: Start imatinib from the mass location and planned resection
answerChoices.rationale: Location and operative morbidity do not establish an imatinib-sensitive GIST or substitute for representative classification.

question.explanation: Interpret the result in relation to what was sampled. question.stem: Which tissue-acquisition plan should be requested next for {patientName}'s treatment planning?
question.explanation: Interpret both the represented layer and the intralesional target. The old superficial sample does not classify the wall lesion; the central fluid region is also different from its enhancing solid component. In this selected preoperative-treatment setting, request EUS-guided core tissue from the solid wall region with subsequent appropriate pathology/molecular workup. This is not a rule to biopsy every straightforward resectable gastric mass.

answerChoices.label: EUS sampling: cores from region B
answerChoices.rationale: The solid component represents the wall lesion and core tissue supports its classification and indicated molecular assessment before selected preoperative treatment.

answerChoices.label: EUS sampling: fluid from region C

answerChoices.rationale: The changed tissue pattern and clinical progression cross the eradication-only management boundary.

answerChoices.label: Another H. pylori eradication course as the current plan
answerChoices.rationale: A negative valid cure assessment and a changed large-cell process do not support treating the new problem as persistent infection.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: A negative valid cure assessment and a changed large-cell process do not support treating the new problem as persistent infection.

answerChoices.label: Scheduled endoscopic observation as the current plan
answerChoices.rationale: Regressing asymptomatic residual disease differs from a growing symptomatic mass with large-cell replacement.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: Regressing asymptomatic residual disease differs from a growing symptomatic mass with large-cell replacement.

question.explanation: The new course is not simple persistence of a small-cell infiltrate or a molecular clone after an improving lesion. A symptomatic enlarging mass with a new large-cell process requires hematology reassessment for lymphoma-directed care. The case does not select one radiotherapy or systemic regimen without staging and specialist review.

exhibit.caption: Original constructed teaching record; fictional patient observations

items.label: Earlier biopsies
items.value: Small B-cell infiltrate with lymphoepithelial lesions; no sheets of large cells.

items.label: Current endoscopy and pathology
items.value: New enlarging ulcerated mass; multiple samples show broad sheets of large atypical B cells replacing the previous small-cell architecture.

items.label: Infection follow-up
items.value: Appropriately timed nonserologic test remains negative after the documented medication washout.

items.label: Prior response
items.value: The original gastric lesion had become smaller before the current deterioration.

case.presentation: {patientName}, a 68-year-old woman, attends the clinic after prior treatment of localized gastric MALT lymphoma with H. pylori eradication. Early follow-up showed regression. She now has worsening early satiety and weight loss.

fields.currentUpdate: After completed eradication, the urea breath test is negative six weeks after treatment started and two weeks after stopping proton-pump inhibitors. proposals.objective: Select additional staging for an advanced diffuse gastric cancer despite CT without distant lesions.
proposals.currentUpdate: The outside team is planning treatment before gastrectomy.
proposals.task: Which additional staging procedure should be arranged for {patientName} before the proposed gastric-cancer treatment sequence?

exhibit.caption: Original constructed teaching record; fictional patient observations

items.label: Endoscopy and biopsy
items.value: Most of the gastric body is rigid and poorly distensible. Multiple biopsies contain poorly cohesive adenocarcinoma.

items.label: Contrast CT chest, abdomen and pelvis
items.value: Diffuse gastric-wall thickening reaches the surrounding fat. Several regional nodes are enlarged. No ascites, peritoneal nodule or distant organ lesion is identified.

choices.label: Staging laparoscopy with peritoneal washings
choices.rationale: The diffuse advanced pattern raises concern for disease that CT may not show on the peritoneal surface. Laparoscopic inspection and washings can alter the intended treatment sequence.
choices.temptation: Look beyond an unrevealing distant-organ CT survey.
choices.counterfactual: A superficial small lesion with an unresolved wall-depth question would instead prioritize local depth assessment.

choices.label: Endoscopic ultrasound with regional-node sampling
choices.rationale: Regional depth and node information would not settle the consequential possibility of occult peritoneal spread in this advanced diffuse presentation.
choices.temptation: Treat more precise local staging as completion of the metastatic assessment.
choices.counterfactual: EUS can be appropriate when uncertain local depth would determine endoscopic versus surgical treatment.

choices.label: Whole-body FDG PET/CT for distant staging
choices.rationale: A metabolic survey does not replace direct peritoneal assessment and cytology in this selected high-risk pattern.
choices.temptation: Use another negative noninvasive survey to clear the proposed pathway.
choices.counterfactual: PET/CT is a useful initial staging tool for the gastric large-B-cell lymphoma tested separately in this packet.

proposals.explanation: Diffuse advanced gastric involvement changes what a negative CT can establish. Laparoscopic peritoneal staging can uncover a treatment-changing distribution before the planned sequence; this is not a rule for every early gastric lesion.

proposals.objective: Apply positive peritoneal cytology obtained before initial treatment to the gastric-cancer treatment sequence.
proposals.currentUpdate: At a later clinic visit, the outside staging-laparoscopy report has arrived. No cancer treatment has begun.
proposals.task: Which treatment sequence should the clinic recommend discussing for {patientName}'s newly returned gastric-cancer staging findings?

exhibit.caption: Original constructed teaching record; fictional patient observations

items.label: Laparoscopic findings
items.value: No visible peritoneal deposit was seen. Washings were collected before manipulation of the primary tumor.

items.label: Cytology
items.value: Malignant epithelial cells with features concordant with the gastric primary are present.

items.label: Current clinical course
items.value: She continues oral intake and has no ongoing bleeding or obstruction.

choices.label: Systemic treatment, then reassess resection candidacy
choices.rationale: The positive washings establish clinically important spread despite an unrevealing visual survey. With this finding obtained before initial treatment, systemic treatment precedes reconsideration of surgery; subsequent clearance can change candidacy.
choices.temptation: Use cytology and its acquisition phase rather than the absence of visible nodules.
choices.counterfactual: If washings and the rest of staging were negative, the ordinary curative-intent multimodality sequence would remain available.

choices.label: Upfront gastrectomy, then postoperative chemotherapy
choices.rationale: This treats a pre-initial-treatment cytology result as if it were a finding discovered during an already undertaken gastrectomy. The chronology matters.
choices.temptation: Equate no visible deposit with a purely localized cancer.
choices.counterfactual: The current Japanese guideline has a different weak recommendation when CY1 is first identified during gastrectomy; that is not this record.

choices.label: Gastric chemoradiation, then reassess resection candidacy
choices.rationale: A stomach-focused treatment strategy does not address the demonstrated peritoneal distribution in the way a systemic-first plan does.
choices.temptation: Treat this as a problem of local tumor control rather than disease distribution.
choices.counterfactual: A nonmetastatic local-control problem can prompt a specialist chemoradiation discussion; it does not reverse positive pre-treatment washings.

proposals.explanation: Positive washings and a negative visual survey are not equivalent staging results. Because cytology was obtained before initial treatment, discuss systemic therapy followed by reassessment rather than immediate gastrectomy. This does not assert that surgery can never become appropriate.

manualAuthorGate.consequence: Ignoring microscopic spread can lead to an inappropriate immediate surgical sequence.

proposals.objective: Choose completion gastric surgery when a clear-margin endoscopic specimen contains lymphatic tumor involvement.
proposals.task: Which management plan should be discussed for {patientName} after review of the gastric endoscopic-resection specimen?

exhibit.caption: Original constructed teaching record; fictional patient observations

items.label: Endoscopic specimen
items.value: An 18-mm differentiated tubular adenocarcinoma was removed en bloc. It is confined to the mucosa, with no ulceration; lateral and deep margins are clear.

items.label: Additional sections
items.value: Separate clusters of epithelial tumor cells lie inside endothelial-lined lymphatic spaces beneath the lesion.

items.label: Staging and health
items.value: CT shows no enlarged regional node or distant lesion. She is independently active and has no major cardiopulmonary disease.

choices.label: Gastrectomy with lymphadenectomy
choices.rationale: The lymphatic tumor finding changes endoscopic curability. A clear scar and normal-size nodes do not eliminate the concern outside the endoscopically removed mucosal field.
choices.temptation: Distinguish removal of the visible lesion from clearance of its nodal-risk pathway.
choices.counterfactual: If lymphatic and vascular invasion were absent and the other stated favorable criteria remained, endoscopic follow-up could be appropriate.

choices.label: Repeat endoscopic submucosal dissection
choices.rationale: More scar resection does not address lymphatic involvement when the existing mucosal resection margins are already clear.
choices.temptation: Treat every noncurative endoscopic result as a local-margin problem.
choices.counterfactual: An isolated favorable horizontal-margin problem can permit further endoscopic treatment after appropriate specimen assessment.

choices.label: Endoscopic and radiologic surveillance
choices.rationale: Surveillance gives excessive weight to the small mucosal lesion, clear margins and CT node size while overlooking the lymphatic finding in a fit patient.
choices.temptation: Assume a clear-margin mucosal cancer is necessarily an endoscopic cure.
choices.counterfactual: A fully curative endoscopic specimen or severe operative comorbidity changes this decision and its counseling.

proposals.explanation: Clear margins answer a local removal question. Tumor within lymphatic spaces changes the concern for disease beyond that field. In this fit patient, completion gastrectomy with lymphadenectomy is the supported discussion despite unrevealing CT nodes.

manualAuthorGate.coverTheKey: The record reports what is seen in lymphatic spaces rather than an eCura label or a statement that surgery is needed. Three specific definitive plans have comparable scope; no key-only availability or preservation preference is supplied.

manualAuthorGate.closestError: Choose surveillance from clear margins, small mucosal size and non-enlarged CT nodes.
manualAuthorGate.decidingObservation: Tumor in lymphatic spaces; margin status and local depth do not remove this finding.
manualAuthorGate.consequence: The patient could retain an untreated regional-risk compartment.
manualAuthorGate.residentDifficulty: Moderate to hard PGY-2/3 prediction from discordant local-clearance and extra-field-risk evidence.
manualAuthorGate.singleDefensibleBestAnswer: Fit patient, clear local margins and lymphatic involvement favor gastrectomy/lymphadenectomy over another local resection or routine surveillance.
manualAuthorGate.counterfactual: Remove lymphatic and vascular invasion while retaining the other favorable pathology: surveillance becomes reasonable; change only the horizontal margin and repeat endoscopic treatment can become reasonable.
deletionTest: Clear margins and mucosal depth create the credible surveillance error.

Fitness establishes applicability of the surgical recommendation; CT node size tests its limited negative value.

proposals.task: Which postoperative treatment should be discussed for {patientName}'s gastric cancer on the basis of the outside operative and pathology records?

exhibit.caption: Original constructed teaching record; fictional patient observations

items.label: Prior treatment
items.value: The outside hospital performed upfront gastrectomy; she received no preoperative drug treatment or radiotherapy.

items.label: Treatment assessment

choices.counterfactual: Severe persistent neuropathy or renal dysfunction would require a different specific regimen assessment; neither is supplied here.

choices.counterfactual: An inadequate lymphadenectomy or involved margin can change the chemoradiation discussion.

choices.counterfactual: Preserved splenic and pancreatic planes with no greater-curvature or hilar involvement would support preservation.

proposals.currentUpdate: The outside team is considering drug treatment before resection if tissue classification supports it.
proposals.task: Which tissue-acquisition route should be requested for {patientName}'s gastric mass before the proposed treatment?

items.label: Contrast CT
items.value: An 8-cm mass is centered in the gastric wall at the cardia. It has a substantial enhancing tissue component and no distant lesion.

items.label: Endoscopy and earlier specimen

items.label: EUS record
items.value: The mass is contiguous with the muscular wall layer and can be reached from the gastric lumen.

proposals.explanation: Stomach-limited distribution does not make an aggressive lymphoma an epithelial gastric-cancer operation or indolent MALT radiation case. manualAuthorGate.coverTheKey: All alternatives are named active oncologic treatments of comparable specificity. No generic referral or uniquely comprehensive plan is keyed. The known diagnosis is necessary for this management question, not a diagnosis-answer disclosure.

reasoningSteps: Interpret limited PET distribution within the established aggressive large-cell histology rather than as persistent indolent MALT.

manualAuthorGate.closestError: Give involved-site radiation because the disease remains local and arose after MALT.
manualAuthorGate.decidingObservation: Confirmed adequate large-cell component in a fit patient, despite only gastric/contiguous disease and without an operative emergency.
manualAuthorGate.consequence: Wrong histology-based care can undertreat aggressive lymphoma or impose unnecessary gastrectomy.

manualAuthorGate.counterfactual: Return the tissue to low-grade MALT with symptomatic progression after eradication: involved-site radiation becomes reasonable. Add uncontrolled perforation or hemorrhage: immediate surgical priorities change.
deletionTest: PET extent makes a local-treatment error credible rather than providing a decorative result.

decisionNodes.stem: Which additional staging procedure should be arranged for {patientName} before the proposed gastric-cancer treatment sequence?

answerChoices.label: Staging laparoscopy with peritoneal washings
answerChoices.rationale: The diffuse advanced pattern raises concern for disease that CT may not show on the peritoneal surface. Laparoscopic inspection and washings can alter the intended treatment sequence.

answerChoices.label: Endoscopic ultrasound with regional-node sampling
answerChoices.rationale: Regional depth and node information would not settle the consequential possibility of occult peritoneal spread in this advanced diffuse presentation.

answerChoices.label: Whole-body FDG PET/CT for distant staging
answerChoices.rationale: A metabolic survey does not replace direct peritoneal assessment and cytology in this selected high-risk pattern.

decisionNodes.explanation: Diffuse advanced gastric involvement changes what a negative CT can establish. Laparoscopic peritoneal staging can uncover a treatment-changing distribution before the planned sequence; this is not a rule for every early gastric lesion.

decisionNodes.stem: Which treatment sequence should the clinic recommend discussing for {patientName}'s newly returned gastric-cancer staging findings?

answerChoices.label: Systemic treatment, then reassess resection candidacy
answerChoices.rationale: The positive washings establish clinically important spread despite an unrevealing visual survey. With this finding obtained before initial treatment, systemic treatment precedes reconsideration of surgery; subsequent clearance can change candidacy.

answerChoices.label: Upfront gastrectomy, then postoperative chemotherapy
answerChoices.rationale: This treats a pre-initial-treatment cytology result as if it were a finding discovered during an already undertaken gastrectomy. The chronology matters.

answerChoices.label: Gastric chemoradiation, then reassess resection candidacy
answerChoices.rationale: A stomach-focused treatment strategy does not address the demonstrated peritoneal distribution in the way a systemic-first plan does.

decisionNodes.explanation: Positive washings and a negative visual survey are not equivalent staging results. Because cytology was obtained before initial treatment, discuss systemic therapy followed by reassessment rather than immediate gastrectomy. This does not assert that surgery can never become appropriate.

decisionNodes.stem: Which management plan should be discussed for {patientName} after review of the gastric endoscopic-resection specimen?

answerChoices.label: Gastrectomy with lymphadenectomy
answerChoices.rationale: The lymphatic tumor finding changes endoscopic curability. A clear scar and normal-size nodes do not eliminate the concern outside the endoscopically removed mucosal field.

answerChoices.label: Repeat endoscopic submucosal dissection
answerChoices.rationale: More scar resection does not address lymphatic involvement when the existing mucosal resection margins are already clear.

answerChoices.label: Endoscopic and radiologic surveillance
answerChoices.rationale: Surveillance gives excessive weight to the small mucosal lesion, clear margins and CT node size while overlooking the lymphatic finding in a fit patient.

decisionNodes.explanation: Clear margins answer a local removal question. Tumor within lymphatic spaces changes the concern for disease beyond that field. In this fit patient, completion gastrectomy with lymphadenectomy is the supported discussion despite unrevealing CT nodes.

decisionNodes.stem: Which postoperative treatment should be discussed for {patientName}'s gastric cancer on the basis of the outside operative and pathology records?

answerChoices.label: Adjuvant CAPOX chemotherapy
answerChoices.rationale: Capecitabine and oxaliplatin are supported after curative D2 surgery for stage II/III disease. This is postoperative treatment after upfront surgery, not selection of a new perioperative regimen.

answerChoices.label: Adjuvant capecitabine chemoradiation
answerChoices.rationale: The completed R0 D2 record lacks the margin or inadequate-dissection boundary that would make a postoperative local-control strategy more compelling.

answerChoices.label: Adjuvant CAPOX plus nivolumab
answerChoices.rationale: The adjuvant nivolumab trial after upfront D2 surgery did not establish added benefit. A newer perioperative immunotherapy approval is not interchangeable with this postoperative-only plan.

decisionNodes.explanation: Match systemic treatment to the pathway that actually occurred. Stage III disease after upfront R0 D2 resection supports adjuvant CAPOX among these options. Adequate dissection and clear margins affect the radiation comparison; postoperative nivolumab is not established by perioperative immunotherapy results.

decisionNodes.stem: Which adjacent-organ extent best fits {patientName}'s documented gastric-cancer operative findings?

answerChoices.label: Gastrectomy with splenectomy
answerChoices.rationale: Splenic involvement is therapeutic resection territory rather than a prophylactic splenectomy scenario. The separately documented pancreatic plane does not support adding distal pancreatectomy.

answerChoices.label: Gastrectomy with pancreatosplenectomy
answerChoices.rationale: This adds removal of an organ whose interface is documented as separate and intact. Splenic involvement does not automatically establish pancreatic invasion.

answerChoices.label: Gastrectomy preserving both organs
answerChoices.rationale: The prophylactic spleen-preservation rule cannot override direct splenic invasion in this represented resectable record.

decisionNodes.explanation: Direct splenic invasion changes the spleen decision; a documented intact pancreatic plane changes the pancreas decision separately. This draft retains the organ-specific objective and does not answer the held question about peeling a treated, inseparable interface.

decisionNodes.stem: Which tissue-acquisition route should be requested for {patientName}'s gastric mass before the proposed treatment?

answerChoices.label: EUS-guided core needle biopsy
answerChoices.rationale: The superficial result does not classify the wall lesion. EUS core sampling can obtain representative tissue for histology and subsequent KIT/PDGFRA assessment before medical treatment.

answerChoices.label: CT-guided transabdominal core biopsy
answerChoices.rationale: A percutaneous biopsy can be appropriate, but the reachable localized gastric mass favors the endoscopic route that avoids traversing the peritoneal cavity.

answerChoices.label: Repeat endoscopic forceps mucosal biopsy
answerChoices.rationale: The intact mucosa and represented superficial layers do not establish that repeating this sampling method would reach the mass requiring classification.

decisionNodes.explanation: Interpret a benign sample in relation to what it contains. This specimen describes superficial mucosa, while the treatment question concerns a deeper wall mass. Representative EUS-guided core tissue and molecular evaluation fit the selected pretreatment pathway; not every resectable GIST needs this sequence.

decisionNodes.stem: Which initial tumor-treatment plan best fits {patientName}'s gastric-mass records?

answerChoices.label: Preoperative imatinib with resection reassessment
answerChoices.rationale: The genotype supports imatinib responsiveness, and the anatomy gives shrinkage a consequential operative purpose. The combination supports a neoadjuvant plan rather than treatment from size alone.

answerChoices.label: Primary gastrectomy with margin-negative resection
answerChoices.rationale: Primary surgery treats the local disease but accepts the represented total-gastrectomy extent before exploring genotype-responsive reduction of that morbidity.

answerChoices.label: Preoperative avapritinib with resection reassessment
answerChoices.rationale: This substitutes a drug associated with another molecular subgroup for an imatinib-responsive KIT exon 11 tumor. Routine preoperative avapritinib is not established here.

decisionNodes.explanation: The molecular result and operative cost must both matter. KIT exon 11 supports imatinib responsiveness, while the cardia involvement gives response a reason to precede resection. Reassess the operation after treatment rather than assuming that every large GIST or every kinase inhibitor has the same pathway.

decisionNodes.stem: Which drug plan best fits {patientName}'s first gastric-GIST response assessment?

answerChoices.label: Continue the current imatinib regimen
answerChoices.rationale: The attenuation and enhancement changes, absence of a new viable-appearing nodule, and clinical improvement support treatment effect despite the modest diameter increase.

answerChoices.label: Escalate the current imatinib regimen
answerChoices.rationale: The supplied pattern does not establish inadequate tumor suppression requiring dose escalation. Diameter change must be interpreted with density and clinical findings.

answerChoices.label: Replace imatinib with sunitinib
answerChoices.rationale: A second-line switch is premature when the integrated record supports response and no intolerance is present.

decisionNodes.explanation: Targeted GIST responses can reduce attenuation before the tumor shrinks. The matched protocol, lower attenuation, loss of enhancing tissue and improved symptoms argue against calling this imatinib failure from diameter alone. Continue the current regimen while following the planned response assessment.

decisionNodes.stem: Which operation best fits {patientName}'s localized gastric tumor?

answerChoices.label: Full-thickness wedge gastrectomy
answerChoices.rationale: A limited resection can remove this peripheral conventional GIST with an intact capsule. Its lymphatic behavior differs from gastric adenocarcinoma, so routine D2 clearance is not required.

answerChoices.label: Total gastrectomy with D2 dissection
answerChoices.rationale: This applies an epithelial gastric-cancer operation and routine nodal strategy to a fundic mesenchymal tumor, with more gastric loss and no stated nodal indication.

answerChoices.label: Endoscopic submucosal enucleation
answerChoices.rationale: Shelling out a muscular-wall GIST does not provide the same assurance of complete excision with an intact capsule and appropriate wall clearance.

decisionNodes.explanation: The biopsy establishes a conventional GIST pattern, and the peripheral fundic anatomy permits a local full-thickness excision. Preserve the capsule and obtain complete removal; do not substitute routine adenocarcinoma lymphadenectomy or shelling out the mass.

decisionNodes.stem: Which next management plan best fits {patientName}'s returned gastric-GIST resection records?

answerChoices.label: Scheduled CT tumor surveillance
answerChoices.rationale: A microscopic margin does not equal rupture or macroscopic residual tumor. Given the limited tumor risk features and major completion operation, review-based surveillance is the best offered plan rather than automatic resection or imatinib for the margin itself.

answerChoices.label: Completion total gastrectomy
answerChoices.rationale: The microscopic edge does not by itself establish benefit sufficient to justify the represented major gastric loss. Low-morbidity re-excision is a different discussion.

answerChoices.label: Adjuvant imatinib treatment
answerChoices.rationale: R1 status alone is not an adjuvant-imatinib criterion. The reported size, gastric site, low mitotic count and absence of rupture do not supply a high-risk indication in this case.

decisionNodes.explanation: Read margin, gross residual tumor and rupture as separate findings. A microscopic edge in an otherwise intact, macroscopically complete resection does not independently require major completion surgery or adjuvant imatinib. The actual re-excision burden and tumor risk support surveillance among these choices.

decisionNodes.stem: Which postoperative plan should be discussed for {patientName}'s completely resected gastric tumor?

answerChoices.label: CT surveillance after complete resection
answerChoices.rationale: The adverse risk features justify close sarcoma follow-up, but do not make an imatinib-resistant driver sensitive. Metastatic avapritinib activity does not establish routine adjuvant benefit after complete resection.

answerChoices.label: Adjuvant imatinib after complete resection
answerChoices.rationale: Size and mitotic activity cannot overcome primary D842V resistance. Adjuvant imatinib is not indicated for this molecular subtype.

answerChoices.label: Adjuvant avapritinib after complete resection
answerChoices.rationale: Selecting an active drug from the metastatic setting does not establish an adjuvant indication in a patient with complete local removal. A clinical trial is a separate discussion.

decisionNodes.explanation: High recurrence risk is not a substitute for a supported adjuvant drug. D842V excludes routine adjuvant imatinib, and the established avapritinib indication concerns unresectable or metastatic disease. Use risk-based surveillance and sarcoma review rather than invent an adjuvant standard.

decisionNodes.stem: Which imatinib plan should be discussed for {patientName} after review of the outside gastric-GIST treatment records?

answerChoices.label: Continue imatinib with tumor surveillance
answerChoices.rationale: The original metastatic state remains relevant despite current radiographic clearance and resection. Effective imatinib is generally maintained rather than stopped using a localized-adjuvant completion rule.

answerChoices.label: Interrupt imatinib with tumor surveillance
answerChoices.rationale: A clear scan and complete metastasectomy do not establish that interrupting an effective systemic treatment is safe in metastatic GIST.

answerChoices.label: Switch to sunitinib with tumor surveillance
answerChoices.rationale: Neither resistance nor intolerance is present to support a second-line switch. Absence of visible tumor is not a progression criterion.

decisionNodes.explanation: A current clear scan does not erase the original biopsy-confirmed metastatic state. Continue effective tolerated imatinib after response and metastatic resection, rather than apply a finite localized-adjuvant stopping rule or switch lines without failure.

answerChoices.label: Whole-body FDG PET/CT staging
answerChoices.rationale: The adequate tissue establishes a new aggressive component rather than uncertain residual low-grade disease. Whole-body distribution now matters for systemic lymphoma treatment planning.

answerChoices.label: EUS gastric-wall and regional-node staging
answerChoices.rationale: Local wall depth can contribute information, but does not provide the systemic distribution assessment needed for this adequately classified aggressive lymphoma.

answerChoices.label: Repeat endoscopy with gastric mapping biopsies
answerChoices.rationale: The intact multiple biopsies and expert assessment already establish the current large-cell component. Repeating gastric acquisition does not address the pending distribution question.

decisionNodes.explanation: The present sample is adequate and differs from the prior low-grade process. This case deliberately differs from the frozen inadequate-biopsy N3 version.

decisionNodes.stem: Which initial treatment should be discussed for {patientName}'s gastric large-B-cell lymphoma after the returned assessment?

answerChoices.label: R-CHOP-based systemic chemotherapy
answerChoices.rationale: The aggressive large-cell histology supports systemic lymphoma therapy even when staging remains gastric and contiguous. R-CHOP is an evidence-supported offered plan; exact cycles and any radiation addition belong to hematology review.

answerChoices.label: Involved-site gastric radiotherapy
answerChoices.rationale: This transfers a localized indolent-MALT treatment pathway to an adequately established aggressive large-B-cell component in a fit patient.

answerChoices.label: Gastrectomy with D2 lymphadenectomy
answerChoices.rationale: The lymphoma histology and absence of a surgical emergency do not support routine epithelial-cancer resection as the initial lymphoma treatment.

decisionNodes.explanation: Stomach-limited distribution does not make an aggressive lymphoma an epithelial gastric-cancer operation or indolent MALT radiation case. In this fit patient without a surgical complication, R-CHOP-based systemic lymphoma treatment is the supported offered approach, with exact regimen details reviewed by hematology.

manualAuthorChecks.coverTheKey: No complaint or task says peritoneal disease, washings or occult metastasis. All three options are staging procedures with comparable labels and wait proposals. The necessary negative CT cannot be deleted merely because it makes the inference possible.
manualAuthorChecks.sameDecisionStageAndCategory: Three additional staging procedures before initial treatment, not a test against a premature operation.
reasoningSteps: Interpret the poorly distensible, diffuse poorly cohesive cancer and extension beyond the wall as an advanced pattern with peritoneal-spread concern.
Recognize that an unrevealing CT does not settle that distribution and choose direct staging with washings.
manualAuthorChecks.closestError: Request PET/CT to clear distant staging after an unrevealing CT.
manualAuthorChecks.decidingObservation: Diffuse rigid gastric-body involvement with extension into surrounding fat despite no CT-visible peritoneal deposits.
manualAuthorChecks.consequence: An unrecognized peritoneal distribution can put the patient into the wrong surgical sequence.
manualAuthorChecks.residentDifficulty: Moderate to hard PGY-2/3 prediction from local staging versus occult distribution; not measured.
manualAuthorChecks.singleDefensibleBestAnswer: Laparoscopy and washings answer the remaining distribution question among the offered procedures in this selected presentation.
manualAuthorChecks.counterfactual: Replace diffuse advanced involvement with a small superficial lesion whose invasion depth is uncertain: EUS becomes a reasonable next staging procedure.
deletionTest: The CT negative establishes the actual staging limitation.
The diffuse endoscopic pattern and poorly cohesive biopsy establish why additional peritoneal assessment is consequential.
The clinic frame supplies patient identity and avoids an inpatient setting requirement.
manualAuthorChecks.sequenceReview: First node; no lavage result or later treatment feedback is visible. Feedback does not announce what positive cytology requires.
manualAuthorChecks.repairAndRecheck: Removed a task that named occult peritoneal disease and removed a statement that laparoscopy was available. Re-solved three staging competitors using the actual pattern and the negative CT. Current direct guideline support is one weak recommendation, explicitly limited in the ledger.

manualAuthorChecks.coverTheKey: The update supplies acquisition chronology without telling the learner its significance. All options specify a treatment sequence; none uniquely says multidisciplinary or individualized care.
manualAuthorChecks.sameDecisionStageAndCategory: Three initial treatment sequences after completed staging.
reasoningSteps: Recognize that concordant malignant peritoneal cytology changes disease distribution despite no visible implant.
Apply the pre-initial-treatment chronology to systemic-first care and later resection reassessment.
manualAuthorChecks.closestError: Proceed to gastrectomy because the laparoscopy showed no nodule.
manualAuthorChecks.decidingObservation: Positive washings obtained before any initial treatment, not a result first discovered during gastrectomy.
manualAuthorChecks.consequence: Ignoring microscopic spread can lead to an inappropriate immediate surgical sequence.
manualAuthorChecks.residentDifficulty: Hard PGY-2/3 prediction because visual/cytologic disagreement and chronology must both be interpreted.
manualAuthorChecks.singleDefensibleBestAnswer: Systemic-first reassessment fits the directly verified current guideline for pre-initial-treatment CY1.
manualAuthorChecks.counterfactual: Changing the discovery phase to an already undertaken gastrectomy changes the cited Japanese recommendation; changing washings to negative removes this reason to defer resection.
deletionTest: Removing the cytology eliminates the management change.
Removing before-treatment chronology makes regional recommendations harder to distinguish fairly.
Intake and bleeding/obstruction observations separate oncologic sequencing from urgent palliation.
