assertions.text: Select representative pretreatment tissue and molecular evaluation for a challenging gastric-wall mass.

Interpret a benign sample in relation to what it contains. This specimen describes superficial mucosa, while the treatment question concerns a deeper wall mass. Representative EUS-guided core tissue and molecular evaluation fit the selected pretreatment pathway; not every resectable GIST needs this sequence.
The superficial result does not classify the wall lesion. EUS core sampling can obtain representative tissue for histology and subsequent KIT/PDGFRA assessment before medical treatment.
If the lesion could not be reached endoscopically, a safe image-guided percutaneous route could be appropriate.
A percutaneous biopsy can be appropriate, but the reachable localized gastric mass favors the endoscopic route that avoids traversing the peritoneal cavity.
An inaccessible gastric route or an accessible metastatic focus could make image-guided percutaneous core sampling preferable.
The intact mucosa and represented superficial layers do not establish that repeating this sampling method would reach the mass requiring classification.
A mucosal lesion or a visibly ulcerated tumor reaching the sampled surface can make targeted forceps biopsy appropriate.

statementMappings.constructedBasis: Original finite fictional patient observations and chronology. Measured values are constructed data, not invented clinical cutoffs, probabilities, weights or waiting durations.

assertions.text: Apply GIST genotype and cardia anatomy to the choice of preoperative targeted treatment.

The molecular result and operative cost must both matter. KIT exon 11 supports imatinib responsiveness, while the cardia involvement gives response a reason to precede resection. Reassess the operation after treatment rather than assuming that every large GIST or every kinase inhibitor has the same pathway.
The genotype supports imatinib responsiveness, and the anatomy gives shrinkage a consequential operative purpose. The combination supports a neoadjuvant plan rather than treatment from size alone.
A similarly genotyped peripheral lesion removable by a small wedge would favor primary surgery rather than automatically adding preoperative treatment.
Primary surgery treats the local disease but accepts the represented total-gastrectomy extent before exploring genotype-responsive reduction of that morbidity.
A straightforward limited resection, an urgent complication or an imatinib-resistant genotype can change the initial plan.
This substitutes a drug associated with another molecular subgroup for an imatinib-responsive KIT exon 11 tumor. Routine preoperative avapritinib is not established here.
PDGFRA D842V with unresectable or metastatic disease supports avapritinib; that is a different genotype and indication.

statementMappings.constructedBasis: Original finite fictional patient observations and chronology. Measured values are constructed data, not invented clinical cutoffs, probabilities, weights or waiting durations.

assertions.text: Interpret paired CT size and attenuation changes before declaring imatinib failure in gastric GIST.

Targeted GIST responses can reduce attenuation before the tumor shrinks. The matched protocol, lower attenuation, loss of enhancing tissue and improved symptoms argue against calling this imatinib failure from diameter alone. Continue the current regimen while following the planned response assessment.
The attenuation and enhancement changes, absence of a new viable-appearing nodule, and clinical improvement support treatment effect despite the modest diameter increase.
A new enhancing intratumoral nodule or unequivocal new disease would prompt reassessment for true progression.
The supplied pattern does not establish inadequate tumor suppression requiring dose escalation. Diameter change must be interpreted with density and clinical findings.
Confirmed progression after review of adherence, interactions and genotype can support escalation in selected GIST settings.
A second-line switch is premature when the integrated record supports response and no intolerance is present.
Confirmed imatinib failure or intolerance can support sunitinib after specialist assessment.

statementMappings.constructedBasis: Original finite fictional patient observations and chronology. Measured values are constructed data, not invented clinical cutoffs, probabilities, weights or waiting durations.

assertions.text: Identify usable previously obtained tumor tissue before requesting a repeat gastric-wall biopsy for genotyping.

Specimen adequacy and referral completeness are different questions. A benign superficial accession cannot classify a deeper mass, but the separately documented tumor core remains usable. Use the identified adequate block for genotyping rather than repeat acquisition from an administrative omission.

The archive establishes both representative tumor identity and assay adequacy. The superficial referral report does not invalidate the separate core specimen, and another acquisition is unnecessary for this question.
If block B were exhausted or had too little tumor for the assay, repeat core acquisition would be justified.
The attached accession represents surface tissue rather than the wall tumor. A technically completed assay on that material would not supply the intended tumor genotype.
If accession A actually contained representative tumor with validated assay adequacy, it could be a usable molecular specimen.
The current record already establishes a usable tumor-containing core block. Repeating acquisition does not resolve a remaining identity or adequacy problem.
An exhausted, wrong-target or inadequate archived specimen would make repeat acquisition appropriate.

statementMappings.constructedBasis: Original finite fictional patient observations and chronology. Measured values are constructed data, not invented clinical cutoffs, probabilities, weights or waiting durations.

assertions.text: Choose a capsule-preserving local operation for a conventional localized gastric GIST rather than epithelial-cancer nodal surgery.

The biopsy establishes a conventional GIST pattern, and the peripheral fundic anatomy permits a local full-thickness excision. Preserve the capsule and obtain complete removal; do not substitute routine adenocarcinoma lymphadenectomy or shelling out the mass.
A limited resection can remove this peripheral conventional GIST with an intact capsule. Its lymphatic behavior differs from gastric adenocarcinoma, so routine D2 clearance is not required.
A cardia-encircling mass requiring major gastric loss could instead justify a molecularly informed preoperative approach.
This applies an epithelial gastric-cancer operation and routine nodal strategy to a fundic mesenchymal tumor, with more gastric loss and no stated nodal indication.
An extensive proximal gastric adenocarcinoma can warrant total gastrectomy with stage-appropriate nodal dissection.
Shelling out a muscular-wall GIST does not provide the same assurance of complete excision with an intact capsule and appropriate wall clearance.
A confidently characterized benign lesion with an appropriate endoscopic dissection plane is a different operative problem; this tumor is not that record.

statementMappings.constructedBasis: Original finite fictional patient observations and chronology. Measured values are constructed data, not invented clinical cutoffs, probabilities, weights or waiting durations.

assertions.text: Distinguish a microscopic GIST margin from gross residual disease or rupture before recommending major completion surgery.

Read margin, gross residual tumor and rupture as separate findings. A microscopic edge in an otherwise intact, macroscopically complete resection does not independently require major completion surgery or adjuvant imatinib. The actual re-excision burden and tumor risk support surveillance among these choices.

A microscopic margin does not equal rupture or macroscopic residual tumor. Given the limited tumor risk features and major completion operation, review-based surveillance is the best offered plan rather than automatic resection or imatinib for the margin itself.
Gross residual disease or a genuinely high-risk imatinib-responsive tumor would change the treatment assessment.
The microscopic edge does not by itself establish benefit sufficient to justify the represented major gastric loss. Low-morbidity re-excision is a different discussion.
Macroscopic residual localized disease for which complete resection is feasible can justify further surgery; a small low-morbidity re-excision also requires separate assessment.
R1 status alone is not an adjuvant-imatinib criterion. The reported size, gastric site, low mitotic count and absence of rupture do not supply a high-risk indication in this case.
A high-risk tumor with an imatinib-responsive genotype or tumor rupture changes the systemic-treatment question.

statementMappings.constructedBasis: Original finite fictional patient observations and chronology. Measured values are constructed data, not invented clinical cutoffs, probabilities, weights or waiting durations.

assertions.text: Use a PDGFRA D842V result to choose initial systemic therapy for metastatic gastric GIST.

Identify the molecular subgroup within metastatic GIST rather than stop at its name. PDGFRA D842V changes the initial drug choice to avapritinib in this unresectable/metastatic indication; a default imatinib sequence would miss the predictive result.
The metastatic setting fits the regulatory indication, and D842V identifies a molecular subgroup for which avapritinib is active while imatinib is not.
A localized completely resected D842V tumor is a different adjuvant setting and does not automatically warrant this treatment.
The usual first-line choice for many metastatic GISTs does not apply to the primary D842V genotype.
A metastatic KIT exon 11 GIST would ordinarily support initial imatinib.
This is not an imatinib-failure sequence, and sunitinib does not solve the primary D842V resistance boundary.
Confirmed imatinib failure in an appropriate non-D842V molecular context can support sunitinib.

statementMappings.constructedBasis: Original finite fictional patient observations and chronology. Measured values are constructed data, not invented clinical cutoffs, probabilities, weights or waiting durations.

assertions.text: Avoid transferring metastatic targeted-therapy efficacy to unproven adjuvant treatment after complete D842V GIST resection.

High recurrence risk is not a substitute for a supported adjuvant drug. D842V excludes routine adjuvant imatinib, and the established avapritinib indication concerns unresectable or metastatic disease. Use risk-based surveillance and sarcoma review rather than invent an adjuvant standard.

The adverse risk features justify close sarcoma follow-up, but do not make an imatinib-resistant driver sensitive. Metastatic avapritinib activity does not establish routine adjuvant benefit after complete resection.
Residual unresectable or metastatic D842V disease would support avapritinib; an imatinib-responsive high-risk resected GIST could support adjuvant imatinib.
Size and mitotic activity cannot overcome primary D842V resistance. Adjuvant imatinib is not indicated for this molecular subtype.
A comparable high-risk GIST with an imatinib-responsive KIT driver would change this decision.
Selecting an active drug from the metastatic setting does not establish an adjuvant indication in a patient with complete local removal. A clinical trial is a separate discussion.
Demonstrated unresectable or metastatic D842V disease fits the verified indication.

statementMappings.constructedBasis: Original finite fictional patient observations and chronology. Measured values are constructed data, not invented clinical cutoffs, probabilities, weights or waiting durations.

assertions.text: Maintain effective imatinib after response and removal of metastatic gastric GIST rather than apply a finite-adjuvant stopping rule.

A current clear scan does not erase the original biopsy-confirmed metastatic state. Continue effective tolerated imatinib after response and metastatic resection, rather than apply a finite localized-adjuvant stopping rule or switch lines without failure.

The original metastatic state remains relevant despite current radiographic clearance and resection. Effective imatinib is generally maintained rather than stopped using a localized-adjuvant completion rule.
Unacceptable toxicity can require treatment modification; a genuinely localized resected tumor has a different finite-adjuvant discussion.
A clear scan and complete metastasectomy do not establish that interrupting an effective systemic treatment is safe in metastatic GIST.
A finite course after resection of genuinely localized disease is a different setting; treatment-limiting toxicity also changes the discussion.
Neither resistance nor intolerance is present to support a second-line switch. Absence of visible tumor is not a progression criterion.
Confirmed imatinib failure or intolerance can make a sunitinib plan appropriate.

statementMappings.constructedBasis: Original finite fictional patient observations and chronology. Measured values are constructed data, not invented clinical cutoffs, probabilities, weights or waiting durations.

assertions.text: Stage a newly documented gastric large-B-cell lymphoma component after adequate tissue classification.

The present sample is adequate and differs from the prior low-grade process. After a large-B-cell component has been established, assess systemic distribution rather than repeat tissue simply because the prior disease was MALT. This case deliberately differs from the frozen inadequate-biopsy N3 version.
The adequate tissue establishes a new aggressive component rather than uncertain residual low-grade disease. Whole-body distribution now matters for systemic lymphoma treatment planning.
An inadequate crushed sample would require diagnostic tissue before assuming the new histology; that frozen N3 case remains separate.
Local wall depth can contribute information, but does not provide the systemic distribution assessment needed for this adequately classified aggressive lymphoma.
A localized low-grade MALT question about wall invasion or regional disease can justify EUS.
The intact multiple biopsies and expert assessment already establish the current large-cell component. Repeating gastric acquisition does not address the pending distribution question.
Scant crushed material unable to establish architecture would justify repeat tissue acquisition.

statementMappings.constructedBasis: Original finite fictional patient observations and chronology. Measured values are constructed data, not invented clinical cutoffs, probabilities, weights or waiting durations.

assertions.text: Select systemic lymphoma treatment for adequately classified gastric large-B-cell disease despite a stomach-limited distribution.

Stomach-limited distribution does not make an aggressive lymphoma an epithelial gastric-cancer operation or indolent MALT radiation case. In this fit patient without a surgical complication, R-CHOP-based systemic lymphoma treatment is the supported offered approach, with exact regimen details reviewed by hematology.

The aggressive large-cell histology supports systemic lymphoma therapy even when staging remains gastric and contiguous. R-CHOP is an evidence-supported offered plan; exact cycles and any radiation addition belong to hematology review.
An indolent localized MALT process after eradication failure can favor involved-site radiation; an acute surgical complication changes immediate priorities.
This transfers a localized indolent-MALT treatment pathway to an adequately established aggressive large-B-cell component in a fit patient.
Symptomatic localized low-grade MALT after adequate eradication and reassessment can warrant involved-site radiotherapy.
The lymphoma histology and absence of a surgical emergency do not support routine epithelial-cancer resection as the initial lymphoma treatment.
Gastric adenocarcinoma with the appropriate stage or an uncontrolled surgical complication is a different operative indication.

rankedConcepts.title: Gastric stage-to-treatment sequence
rankedConcepts.decision: Choose staging before committing to a treatment pathway; interpret washings in their acquisition phase.
rankedConcepts.rawEvidence: Diffuse poorly cohesive tumor, CT extent, laparoscopic survey, concordant washings obtained before initial treatment.
rankedConcepts.closestCredibleError: Treat no visible metastasis as absence of spread or apply a during-gastrectomy rule to pre-treatment cytology.
rankedConcepts.coverage: Major live gap covered by two-node case.
rankedConcepts.testingRelevance: Central resident oncologic planning with a concrete change in action; qualitative editorial priority, not an exam frequency claim.

rankedConcepts.title: Endoscopic curability versus local clearance
rankedConcepts.decision: Decide when a clear-margin gastric ESD still needs lymphadenectomy.
rankedConcepts.rawEvidence: Depth, differentiation, ulceration, actual lymphatic involvement, margins, CT nodes and operative fitness.
rankedConcepts.closestCredibleError: Equate local R0 removal or normal-size nodes with endoscopic cure.
rankedConcepts.testingRelevance: Tests pathology-to-operation reasoning and the limits of a reassuring scan.

rankedConcepts.title: Postoperative evidence after upfront D2 surgery
rankedConcepts.decision: Choose a postoperative regimen from the pathway that actually occurred.
rankedConcepts.rawEvidence: Stage III, R0/D2 record, no preoperative therapy, retained mismatch-repair proteins and treatment fitness.
rankedConcepts.closestCredibleError: Transfer perioperative/metastatic immunotherapy or an inadequate-dissection radiation rule into a different completed pathway.
rankedConcepts.consequence: Unestablished additional treatment/toxicity or wrong evidence setting.
rankedConcepts.coverage: Gap covered for one defined postoperative setting; current preoperative regimen ranking remains unkeyed research only.
rankedConcepts.testingRelevance: Stage, surgery quality and treatment phase are testable surgical oncology decisions.

rankedConcepts.title: Therapeutic organ resection versus prophylactic organ removal
rankedConcepts.decision: Select the organ-specific extent instead of applying one blanket preservation/removal rule.
rankedConcepts.rawEvidence: Separate splenic parenchymal invasion, intact pancreatic plane, completed metastatic assessment and R0 feasibility.
rankedConcepts.closestCredibleError: Apply routine spleen preservation despite invasion or automatically remove pancreas with spleen.
rankedConcepts.coverage: Redundant earlier versions audited; one stable-meaning rewrite. Treated inseparable-interface rule remains held.
rankedConcepts.testingRelevance: Practical extent decisions and a close prophylactic-versus-therapeutic misconception.

rankedConcepts.title: GIST tissue, genotype and operative sequence
rankedConcepts.decision: Choose representative pretreatment tissue, then use actual driver and operative anatomy to select therapy.
rankedConcepts.rawEvidence: Sample layers, reachable EUS wall mass, KIT exon 11 and cardia encirclement.
rankedConcepts.closestCredibleError: Accept benign overlying mucosa or a supplied sensitivity label; treat every localized GIST with immediate major resection.
rankedConcepts.consequence: Wrong treatment or avoidable gastric loss.
rankedConcepts.coverage: Nine live variants overconcentrate on two cues; two stable-meaning rewrites plus a new response companion.
rankedConcepts.testingRelevance: High-value integration of diagnosis, predictive pathology and actual operative cost.

rankedConcepts.title: GIST response assessment
rankedConcepts.decision: Choose drug continuation versus a resistance pathway from matched imaging.
rankedConcepts.rawEvidence: Diameter, attenuation, enhancement, protocol matching, new nodules and symptoms.
rankedConcepts.closestCredibleError: Read a modest larger diameter as treatment failure.
rankedConcepts.coverage: New gap covered as a third node after treatment selection.
rankedConcepts.testingRelevance: A clinically consequential imaging-interpretation error rather than a report label.

rankedConcepts.title: Conventional localized GIST surgery
rankedConcepts.decision: Choose adequate capsule-preserving local excision without routine epithelial-cancer nodal surgery.
rankedConcepts.rawEvidence: DOG1/CD117 and genotype, retained SDHB, fundic site, relation to cardia/adjacent organs and nodes.
rankedConcepts.closestCredibleError: Use enucleation or total gastrectomy/D2 as universal gastric-tumor surgery.
rankedConcepts.consequence: Inadequate excision or avoidable major resection.
rankedConcepts.testingRelevance: Core technical-oncologic distinction that changes the operation.

rankedConcepts.title: Microscopic GIST margin versus rupture
rankedConcepts.decision: Weigh surveillance, major completion surgery and systemic treatment after R1.
rankedConcepts.rawEvidence: Actual rupture/spill/gross-remnant record, size, site, mitoses and proposed completion extent.
rankedConcepts.closestCredibleError: Treat any positive microscopic edge as gross residual disease or metastatic risk.
rankedConcepts.coverage: New gap covered with a paired postoperative node; rupture duration is not guessed.
rankedConcepts.testingRelevance: Close adverse-pathology boundary with substantial morbidity consequences.

rankedConcepts.title: Molecular treatment setting in GIST
rankedConcepts.decision: Distinguish metastatic D842V drug selection from completely resected D842V care.
rankedConcepts.rawEvidence: PDGFRA exon 18 D842V, tissue-concordant metastasis or complete intact resection.
rankedConcepts.closestCredibleError: Default to imatinib or transfer avapritinib efficacy into unproven routine adjuvant treatment.
rankedConcepts.coverage: Two new complementary standalone meanings; do not serve one as preceding feedback for the other.
rankedConcepts.testingRelevance: Predictive genotype and evidence-setting boundaries are testable; no dose trivia or invented duration.

rankedConcepts.title: Metastatic GIST treatment after apparent remission
rankedConcepts.decision: Choose continuation rather than a localized-adjuvant stopping rule.
rankedConcepts.rawEvidence: Original biopsy-proven liver metastasis, response, complete resection, clear current imaging and tolerance.
rankedConcepts.closestCredibleError: Erase metastatic status after a clear scan.
rankedConcepts.testingRelevance: Longitudinal disease-state reasoning with a real medication consequence.

rankedConcepts.title: Integrated MALT diagnosis and transformation boundary
rankedConcepts.decision: Distinguish architecture from lineage/clonality and scattered versus confluent large cells.
rankedConcepts.rawEvidence: Gland relationships, small-cell morphology, marker panel, molecular-test result and large-cell arrangement.
rankedConcepts.closestCredibleError: Count CD20 or clonality as a diagnosis; overcall scattered large cells or let negative fusion testing exclude MALT.
rankedConcepts.coverage: Heavy historic redundancy; exact approved originals and B24/B25-context/B30 PASS versions retained. No cosmetic additional variant.
rankedConcepts.testingRelevance: Important recognition must have a practical treatment or evidence consequence.

rankedConcepts.title: MALT response-dependent care
rankedConcepts.decision: Select observation versus involved-site radiation from actual post-eradication course.
rankedConcepts.rawEvidence: Interpretable infection test, symptoms, ulcer evolution, fibrosis, low-grade burden and persistent clone.
rankedConcepts.closestCredibleError: Equate residual clonality with failure or observe overt progression.
rankedConcepts.coverage: Existing frozen B25/B30-context PASS already cover the consequential contrast. Initial-treatment originals stay historically approved.
rankedConcepts.testingRelevance: Trajectory is more testable than another memorized eradication-first label.

rankedConcepts.title: Changed gastric lymphoma: adequacy, staging and treatment
rankedConcepts.decision: Decide when to resample versus stage, then select histology-specific therapy.
rankedConcepts.rawEvidence: Scant crushed tissue versus intact confluent large-cell tissue; PET distribution, fitness, infection and surgical complications.
rankedConcepts.closestCredibleError: Anchor on old MALT; repeat adequate tissue; apply local-only treatment because distribution is limited.
rankedConcepts.coverage: Frozen N3 inadequate-sample PASS retained; new adequate-sample two-node case supplies staging and named treatment.
rankedConcepts.testingRelevance: Reverses a real adequacy boundary and forces reassessment of histology and treatment phase.

rankedConcepts.title: Existing tumor tissue versus missing referral material
rankedConcepts.decision: Select the correctly identified adequate archived specimen before repeating acquisition.
rankedConcepts.rawEvidence: Two accessions, represented layers, procedure-site match and remaining tumor/assay adequacy.
rankedConcepts.closestCredibleError: Treat incomplete referral paperwork as absent tissue or genotype a benign surface sample.
rankedConcepts.coverage: Old target-map v2 remains REVISE. New changed-meaning draft with explicit prior identity; reviewer must assess difficulty.
rankedConcepts.testingRelevance: Organ-specific provenance has a practical diagnostic and procedural consequence.

rankedConcepts.title: Remaining gastric-cancer operative and palliation gaps
rankedConcepts.decision: Assess extent of gastrectomy/margins and obstruction palliation using explicit goals.
rankedConcepts.rawEvidence: Mapped extent, histology, margin assessment, obstruction severity and expected treatment course.
rankedConcepts.closestCredibleError: Assume total surgery, stent or bypass is universally preferable.
rankedConcepts.coverage: Not drafted: no fully verified close same-stage comparison with all patient-specific eligibility criteria established in this lane.
rankedConcepts.testingRelevance: Consequential next research work; do not manufacture survival cutoffs, stent thresholds or margin distances.

ownerApprovalsNeeded.question: Confirm the systemic-first key for positive washings obtained before initial treatment, and its intended US-clinic application rather than the different during-gastrectomy CY1 recommendation.
ownerApprovalsNeeded.boundary: One directly verified current Japanese guideline for this exact chronology; no permanent prohibition on later surgery.

competingActions: Separate the treated interface and preserve adjacent organs
ownerApprovalsNeeded.question: What exact oncologic-plane/resectability evidence would justify either action for the old proven-invasion then treated inseparable-interface case?
ownerApprovalsNeeded.boundary: Original source hold remains. Current direct-invasion guidance does not verify the precise post-treatment comparison; no newly keyed item for that held point.

competingActions: Molecular testing from identified adequate archived tumor
ownerApprovalsNeeded.question: For the new archived-tissue draft, confirm the supplied identity/adequacy data justify using B and that the specimen reasoning is sufficiently consequential. The old region-picking item remains REVISE.
ownerApprovalsNeeded.boundary: Tissue banking and molecular guidance support the new application; the exact comparison is constructed specimen logic. Independent editorial review must reassess difficulty.

sourceReview.title: Additional staging of diffuse gastric adenocarcinoma
fairness: Laparoscopy with washings is the single best offered procedure for this diffuse, locally advanced pattern despite CT without visible metastases. EUS addresses locoregional detail, and PET/CT does not settle occult peritoneal involvement. The necessary negative CT is data, not an unfair exclusion.

Two consequential steps remain: interpret the diffuse poorly cohesive cancer and extramural findings, then choose the staging method that can change the proposed treatment sequence. This is a high-yield gastric-cancer staging decision.
The first node is self-contained. Its explanation prepares the importance of peritoneal staging without giving the later positive-cytology treatment answer.

Review scope for this entire report: all 16 candidate nodes, comprising four rewrites and twelve new items. The 17 kept records, 28 retirement proposals, recorded holds and parked alternatives were noted but not adjudicated. Clinical judgments are offline assessments of the supplied visible fields, not fresh source verification or clinical sign-off. Difficulty and highYield are qualitative judgments, not measured performance or verified exam frequencies. Runtime rendering, waits and source-ledger accuracy were not tested.

sourceReview.title: Treatment sequence after positive peritoneal cytology
fairness: Concordant malignant cells establish peritoneal involvement despite a negative visual survey. No treatment has begun and no bleeding or obstructive indication for palliation is supplied; systemic treatment followed by reassessment is the best offered sequence.

The real competing error is proceeding with gastrectomy because no macroscopic deposits were seen. Interpreting the discordant staging observations and changing treatment intent/sequence are two consequential steps.

Chronology follows the first node coherently. The shared presentation, current update and cytology exhibit supply the facts needed without remembering the earlier CT. Prior feedback does not specify this answer.

The explanation appropriately leaves later surgery conditional; it does not promise conversion to resectability or prescribe an unsupported regimen. No confident clinical inaccuracy identified in this offline review.

sourceReview.title: Lymphatic invasion after apparently complete endoscopic resection
fairness: Lymphatic tumor involvement overrides the otherwise reassuring mucosal depth, small size and clear margins. In the stated fit patient, gastrectomy with lymphadenectomy is the single best offered plan. Repeating local excision does not address the relevant risk.

The microscopic description requires interpretation followed by distinguishing local clearance from potential nodal disease. Surveillance remains a meaningful temptation because the other reported features favor endoscopic curability.

Lymphatic spaces and lymphadenectomy share a word root, but that relationship alone cannot distinguish appropriate nodal treatment from management of a fully excised primary; this is necessary clinical evidence rather than a decisive nonmedical cue.
Self-contained presentation and complete task; no preceding answer is needed. High-yield gastric endoscopic-curability boundary. No confident clinical inaccuracy identified.

sourceReview.title: Adjuvant treatment after upfront R0 D2 gastrectomy
fairness: Among the offered choices, CAPOX is defensible after upfront clear-margin D2 resection of stage III disease in this recovered patient. The extent of dissection and absence of preoperative treatment make the radiation and perioperative-treatment extrapolation errors consequential.

Retained mismatch-repair proteins, renal function and neuropathy assessment address relevant treatment modifiers. The question supplies final stage rather than asking the learner to reconstruct it from an unspecified positive-node count; that is fair for this management objective.
The repeated CAPOX component does not uniquely identify the key: deciding whether to add nivolumab still requires knowledge. All options are comparably specific postoperative regimens.

Self-contained and high yield. No confident inaccuracy identified, but the time-sensitive immunotherapy/adjuvant boundary has not been freshly verified under the no-network constraint; editorial PASS is not clinical approval.

cues.why: Completes an option-by-option elimination template. These are legitimate operative findings, but the present three choices turn them into direct answer assembly rather than two consequential inferences.

fairness: Gastrectomy with splenectomy is the defensible key for the stated direct splenic invasion and separate intact pancreas. I am not alleging an inaccurate key or recommending removal of necessary invasion/plane findings.

Two organ decisions are applications of the same supplied involvement rule, not two reasoning steps. The underlying distinction between indicated en-bloc resection and prophylactic adjacent-organ removal is high yield.
The clinic review frame is coherent and stands alone; the explanation, not the patient chronology, is the clarity problem.

The core operational lesson is sensible, but this particular administrative reconciliation has less ABSITE/boards yield than genotype-dependent GIST management or representative tissue acquisition. highYield=false refers to this scored task, not to the importance of specimen identity.
There is no second consequential inference after the laboratory has confirmed identity, representation and assay adequacy. The item stands alone and has no later part.
suggestions: Describe an incomplete referral attachment rather than imply two contradictory diagnoses.

Consider merging this into post-answer teaching for the tissue-acquisition item. If retained as a scored item, supply a real specimen-target or adequacy distinction that the resident must interpret, while preserving enough information for one fair answer.
Do not withhold a laboratory fact and require residents to guess a local molecular-test adequacy threshold.

sourceReview.title: Operation for a localized peripheral gastric GIST
fairness: The immunophenotype supports GIST, and the peripheral 3.2-cm fundic anatomy supports full-thickness wedge resection rather than total gastrectomy/D2 or submucosal shelling out. Histology and anatomy must both inform the operative choice.

The distractors represent confusing GIST with gastric adenocarcinoma and confusing local resection with enucleation. They are easier than the closest specialist alternatives, but remain recognizable resident errors for a high-yield surgical principle.

The presentation explicitly frames retrospective review of a tumor and its later resection, so the initial operation question and subsequent margin review are coherent. The first item supplies its own pathology and anatomy.

No decisive wording-only cue or confident clinical inaccuracy identified. Negative nodes do not alone establish that lymphadenectomy is unnecessary; the learner still needs the tumor-type distinction.

sourceReview.title: Microscopic GIST margin versus rupture and recurrence risk
fairness: The supplied gastric site, 3.2-cm size, low mitotic count, intact removal and absence of gross residual disease distinguish a microscopic positive edge from rupture or a high-risk residual-disease situation. With completion total gastrectomy required, surveillance is the best offered plan.

Both major completion surgery and automatic adjuvant imatinib are credible responses to a positive margin that the learner must reconsider using tumor risk and re-excision burden. These are genuinely consequential linked interpretations.

The postoperative narrowing is a new operative consequence, not a contradiction of the earlier tumor not encircling the cardia. The second node repeats the tumor type, size, mitoses and margin/rupture findings and can be answered independently.

Earlier advice to obtain complete removal does not tell the learner how to manage a microscopic edge afterward. The explanation appropriately avoids claiming every R1 GIST needs neither re-excision nor treatment. No confident clinical inaccuracy identified.

sourceReview.title: Initial drug for metastatic PDGFRA D842V GIST
fairness: Avapritinib is the defensible offered initial drug for metastatic GIST with the specified D842V alteration. Imatinib and sunitinib are plausible general-GIST defaults but do not resolve this predictive genotype. No confident clinical inaccuracy identified; current drug indications were not freshly verified offline.

The metastatic tissue match establishes the treatment setting, but the task already requests an initial systemic drug and all options are drugs. The scored choice collapses to D842V-to-avapritinib recall; recognizing the tumor first does not add a separate consequential decision.
Options are parallel, similarly specific and free of a decisive wording-only shortcut. Moderate difficulty reflects knowing a targeted-therapy exception, not two-step reasoning.
Self-contained and high-yield molecular-treatment exception; the easy-to-identify weakness is cognitive structure, not fairness of the key.
suggestions: Integrate the mutation with a competing disease-setting or treatment-history decision that actually changes eligibility for the offered plan, using verified facts.

Consider consolidating with the resected-D842V item, which already makes metastatic versus adjuvant applicability consequential. Alternatively request explicit acceptance as focused recall; do not describe a diagnosis-plus-drug association as two-step reasoning.

sourceReview.title: Adjuvant boundary after resection of high-risk D842V GIST
fairness: Size and mitotic activity create a real temptation to recommend adjuvant treatment, but D842V makes routine imatinib inappropriate and metastatic-drug efficacy does not establish an adjuvant avapritinib standard. Surveillance is the defensible offered plan after intact complete resection.

The learner must first interpret recurrence risk, then apply mutation-specific sensitivity and the difference between metastatic and adjuvant evidence. Removing either risk or genotype changes the meaningful comparison.
The repeated phrase "after complete resection" is shared across all choices and does not uniquely cue the key. Surveillance is a named plan rather than a vague individualized-management answer.

Self-contained and high yield. No confident clinical inaccuracy identified, but the absence of an established adjuvant targeted-drug indication is time-sensitive and not freshly source-verified under the no-network restriction. This PASS remains an editorial assessment requiring clinician sign-off.

sourceReview.title: Continuing systemic treatment after metastatic GIST resection

cues.phrase: Which imatinib plan should be discussed
cues.why: Names the current drug while one choice switches to sunitinib, making that option a category outlier before the original metastatic state is interpreted.
Directly deprives the sunitinib-switch option of a reason. Those observations are needed for fairness, but this particular distractor becomes disposable.

fairness: Continuing effective, tolerated imatinib is defensible despite a clear current scan after resection of previously metastatic disease. Stopping because all visible disease was removed is the important competing error.

Interpreting original disease status despite current no-evidence-of-disease findings, then distinguishing ongoing metastatic therapy from a finite adjuvant course, are two consequential steps and a high-yield concept.

Switching to sunitinib is much weaker than the continuation-versus-stopping decision because there is no failure or intolerance. The item needs stronger competition, not omitted safety/tolerance facts.
The chronology is self-contained and coherent. No confident clinical inaccuracy identified.
suggestions: Use a neutral task such as which ongoing systemic-treatment plan fits the records.

Replace the unsupported line switch with a credible finite-adjuvant versus metastatic-continuation error. Supply any prior duration only if needed and adequately supported; do not invent a stopping interval.
Preserve the original biopsy-proven metastasis, current clear scan and tolerability so the resulting distinction remains fair.

sourceReview.title: Staging a newly established gastric large-B-cell process
clarityIssues: "Under documented testing conditions" does not identify what made the H. pylori test reliable. The result is not needed to select PET/CT for the already established aggressive lymphoma; the vague phrase adds no decision information here.

The explanation includes an internal reference: "This case deliberately differs from the frozen inadequate-biopsy N3 version." That version is not part of the clinical story and should not appear in learner feedback.

cues.why: Together with expert confirmation of the large-B-cell component, this eliminates the repeat-biopsy alternative by an explicit adequacy signal rather than a disputed specimen finding.

cues.phrase: Expert hematopathology review confirms an aggressive large-B-cell component.
cues.why: Supplies the diagnosis and removes the principal interpretive step. A known diagnosis is legitimate for management, but the remaining task is direct recall of systemic staging versus local staging.

fairness: PET/CT is the defensible staging investigation for the established aggressive large-B-cell process. Repeat mapping and local EUS do not provide equivalent systemic distribution assessment. No confident clinical inaccuracy identified.
Normal blood counts, absence of palpable nodes and H. pylori status do not make systemic staging unnecessary. These data do not create a second consequential inference in this option set.

The prior MALT history is coherent, and the first node stands alone. The later explanation should not refer to unrelated frozen versions. High-yield staging principle, but the current item is one-step recognition after an explicitly confirmed diagnosis.
suggestions: Remove the frozen-N3 editorial sentence and unnecessary infection-testing detail from this staging node.

If retaining a two-step objective, use a genuine unresolved distribution or specimen-interpretation issue whose supported findings change the next staging action. Do not simply remove diagnostic adequacy and make the question ambiguous.
Otherwise seek explicit acceptance as a basic staging item rather than inflate difficulty by retaining the old MALT backstory.

sourceReview.title: Treatment of localized gastric large-B-cell lymphoma

cues.why: The task names the diagnostic category after the preceding node and explanation have established the aggressive process. It is legitimate management context, but the two alternatives are treatments associated with different gastric tumor paradigms, leaving a straightforward disease-to-regimen match.

cues.phrase: There is no perforation, ongoing hemorrhage or obstruction.
cues.why: Appropriately excludes a surgical emergency, but also strips the gastrectomy distractor of its only plausible immediate role. Keeping this necessary information requires a better competing plan, not deleting safety facts.

fairness: R-CHOP-based systemic treatment is defensible among these choices for the fit patient with an established large-B-cell component and no surgical complication. Radiation as the entire offered initial treatment and gastrectomy/D2 are not equivalent alternatives. Exact regimen selection remains for hematology; no confident clinical inaccuracy identified.

The stage and cardiac assessment are relevant clinically, but most of the decision follows simply from the supplied diagnosis. Even without the PET distribution, systemic lymphoma therapy remains the clear answer against these two alternatives. The staging return does not earn a distinct scored inference.

The follow-up is coherent and repeats sufficient diagnosis and fitness information to stand alone. The preceding explanation reinforces the aggressive-versus-MALT distinction, further reducing independent difficulty.
The disease-treatment distinction is high yield, but the current item does not meet the requested two-step resident challenge.
suggestions: Compare credible plans within treatment of established aggressive gastric lymphoma, using stage or fitness data that actually determine the best choice and verified criteria for any finer regimen distinction.
Alternatively keep this as explicitly accepted foundational treatment recognition. Do not add unrelated complexity or remove the urgent-complication screen just to make surgery seem plausible.

choices.label: Staging laparoscopy with peritoneal washings
choices.rationale: The diffuse advanced pattern raises concern for disease that CT may not show on the peritoneal surface. Laparoscopic inspection and washings can alter the intended treatment sequence.
choices.temptation: Look beyond an unrevealing distant-organ CT survey.
choices.counterfactual: A superficial small lesion with an unresolved wall-depth question would instead prioritize local depth assessment.

choices.label: Endoscopic ultrasound with regional-node sampling
choices.rationale: Regional depth and node information would not settle the consequential possibility of occult peritoneal spread in this advanced diffuse presentation.
choices.temptation: Treat more precise local staging as completion of the metastatic assessment.
choices.counterfactual: EUS can be appropriate when uncertain local depth would determine endoscopic versus surgical treatment.

choices.label: Whole-body FDG PET/CT for distant staging
choices.rationale: A metabolic survey does not replace direct peritoneal assessment and cytology in this selected high-risk pattern.
choices.temptation: Use another negative noninvasive survey to clear the proposed pathway.
choices.counterfactual: PET/CT is a useful initial staging tool for the gastric large-B-cell lymphoma tested separately in this packet.

proposal.explanation: Diffuse advanced gastric involvement changes what a negative CT can establish. Laparoscopic peritoneal staging can uncover a treatment-changing distribution before the planned sequence; this is not a rule for every early gastric lesion.

manualAuthorGate.coverTheKey: No complaint or task says peritoneal disease, washings or occult metastasis. All three options are staging procedures with comparable labels and wait proposals. The necessary negative CT cannot be deleted merely because it makes the inference possible.
manualAuthorGate.sameDecisionStageAndCategory: Three additional staging procedures before initial treatment, not a test against a premature operation.
reasoningSteps: Interpret the poorly distensible, diffuse poorly cohesive cancer and extension beyond the wall as an advanced pattern with peritoneal-spread concern.
Recognize that an unrevealing CT does not settle that distribution and choose direct staging with washings.
manualAuthorGate.closestError: Request PET/CT to clear distant staging after an unrevealing CT.
manualAuthorGate.decidingObservation: Diffuse rigid gastric-body involvement with extension into surrounding fat despite no CT-visible peritoneal deposits.
manualAuthorGate.consequence: An unrecognized peritoneal distribution can put the patient into the wrong surgical sequence.
manualAuthorGate.residentDifficulty: Moderate to hard PGY-2/3 prediction from local staging versus occult distribution; not measured.
manualAuthorGate.singleDefensibleBestAnswer: Laparoscopy and washings answer the remaining distribution question among the offered procedures in this selected presentation.
manualAuthorGate.counterfactual: Replace diffuse advanced involvement with a small superficial lesion whose invasion depth is uncertain: EUS becomes a reasonable next staging procedure.
deletionTest: The CT negative establishes the actual staging limitation.
The diffuse endoscopic pattern and poorly cohesive biopsy establish why additional peritoneal assessment is consequential.
The clinic frame supplies patient identity and avoids an inpatient setting requirement.
manualAuthorGate.sequenceReview: First node; no lavage result or later treatment feedback is visible. Feedback does not announce what positive cytology requires.
manualAuthorGate.repairAndRecheck: Removed a task that named occult peritoneal disease and removed a statement that laparoscopy was available. Re-solved three staging competitors using the actual pattern and the negative CT. Current direct guideline support is one weak recommendation, explicitly limited in the ledger.

editorialDisposition.preservation: Exact reviewed artifacts preserved without any wording, profile, exhibit, option, feedback, node-order or rubric change.

fairness.issue: Laparoscopy with washings is the single best offered procedure for this diffuse, locally advanced pattern despite CT without visible metastases. EUS addresses locoregional detail, and PET/CT does not settle occult peritoneal involvement. The necessary negative CT is data, not an unfair exclusion.
fairness.disposition: Exact reviewed artifacts preserved without any wording, profile, exhibit, option, feedback, node-order or rubric change.

fairness.issue: Two consequential steps remain: interpret the diffuse poorly cohesive cancer and extramural findings, then choose the staging method that can change the proposed treatment sequence. This is a high-yield gastric-cancer staging decision.
fairness.disposition: Exact reviewed artifacts preserved without any wording, profile, exhibit, option, feedback, node-order or rubric change.

fairness.issue: The first node is self-contained. Its explanation prepares the importance of peritoneal staging without giving the later positive-cytology treatment answer.

manualAuthorGate.coverTheKey: The record reports what is seen in lymphatic spaces rather than an eCura label or a statement that surgery is needed. Three specific definitive plans have comparable scope; no key-only availability or preservation preference is supplied.

manualAuthorGate.closestError: Choose surveillance from clear margins, small mucosal size and non-enlarged CT nodes.
manualAuthorGate.decidingObservation: Tumor in lymphatic spaces; margin status and local depth do not remove this finding.

manualAuthorGate.singleDefensibleBestAnswer: Fit patient, clear local margins and lymphatic involvement favor gastrectomy/lymphadenectomy over another local resection or routine surveillance.
manualAuthorGate.counterfactual: Remove lymphatic and vascular invasion while retaining the other favorable pathology: surveillance becomes reasonable; change only the horizontal margin and repeat endoscopic treatment can become reasonable.
deletionTest: Clear margins and mucosal depth create the credible surveillance error.

exhibit.caption: Original constructed teaching record; fictional patient observations

items.label: Prior treatment
items.value: The outside hospital performed upfront gastrectomy; she received no preoperative drug treatment or radiotherapy.

items.label: Operation and pathology
items.value: D2 dissection is documented with clear gastric margins. The primary extends into subserosa, and regional nodes contain carcinoma; the final pathology stage is III.

items.label: Treatment assessment
items.value: Mismatch-repair proteins are retained. She has recovered oral intake, with preserved renal function and no function-limiting neuropathy.

answerChoices.label: Adjuvant CAPOX chemotherapy
answerChoices.rationale: Capecitabine and oxaliplatin are supported after curative D2 surgery for stage II/III disease. This is postoperative treatment after upfront surgery, not selection of a new perioperative regimen.

answerChoices.label: Adjuvant capecitabine chemoradiation
answerChoices.rationale: The completed R0 D2 record lacks the margin or inadequate-dissection boundary that would make a postoperative local-control strategy more compelling.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: The completed R0 D2 record lacks the margin or inadequate-dissection boundary that would make a postoperative local-control strategy more compelling.

answerChoices.label: Adjuvant CAPOX plus nivolumab
answerChoices.rationale: The adjuvant nivolumab trial after upfront D2 surgery did not establish added benefit. A newer perioperative immunotherapy approval is not interchangeable with this postoperative-only plan.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: The adjuvant nivolumab trial after upfront D2 surgery did not establish added benefit. A newer perioperative immunotherapy approval is not interchangeable with this postoperative-only plan.

choices.label: Adjuvant CAPOX chemotherapy
choices.rationale: Capecitabine and oxaliplatin are supported after curative D2 surgery for stage II/III disease. This is postoperative treatment after upfront surgery, not selection of a new perioperative regimen.
choices.temptation: Apply evidence to the actual completed treatment phase and dissection.
choices.counterfactual: Severe persistent neuropathy or renal dysfunction would require a different specific regimen assessment; neither is supplied here.

choices.label: Adjuvant capecitabine chemoradiation
choices.rationale: The completed R0 D2 record lacks the margin or inadequate-dissection boundary that would make a postoperative local-control strategy more compelling.
choices.temptation: Apply an older postoperative chemoradiation pathway without checking resection quality.
choices.counterfactual: An inadequate lymphadenectomy or involved margin can change the chemoradiation discussion.

choices.label: Adjuvant CAPOX plus nivolumab
choices.rationale: The adjuvant nivolumab trial after upfront D2 surgery did not establish added benefit. A newer perioperative immunotherapy approval is not interchangeable with this postoperative-only plan.
choices.temptation: Extrapolate metastatic or perioperative immunotherapy success into an untested treatment phase.
choices.counterfactual: A patient beginning an indicated perioperative immunotherapy regimen before surgery represents a different evidence setting; the current FDA update is recorded separately.

proposal.explanation: Match systemic treatment to the pathway that actually occurred. Stage III disease after upfront R0 D2 resection supports adjuvant CAPOX among these options. Adequate dissection and clear margins affect the radiation comparison; postoperative nivolumab is not established by perioperative immunotherapy results.

manualAuthorGate.coverTheKey: Every option is a named postoperative treatment. CAPOX appears in two options, defeating simple regimen-name matching; the longest option is not the key. The chart does not announce which guideline applies.
manualAuthorGate.sameDecisionStageAndCategory: Three postoperative oncologic regimens after completed upfront surgery.
reasoningSteps: Interpret the node-positive stage III specimen as a systemic-recurrence problem despite R0 removal.
Use the D2 record and absence of preoperative therapy to distinguish adjuvant chemotherapy from routine chemoradiation or a perioperative-immunotherapy extrapolation.
manualAuthorGate.closestError: Add immunotherapy because it helps in a different gastric-cancer treatment phase.
manualAuthorGate.decidingObservation: Upfront R0 D2 gastrectomy with no preoperative systemic therapy; the retained mismatch-repair pattern avoids a separate disputed MSI-H adjuvant boundary.
manualAuthorGate.consequence: An evidence mismatch can add toxicity without established benefit or substitute an unsuitable pathway.
manualAuthorGate.residentDifficulty: Hard PGY-2/3 prediction from treatment-phase transfer and dissection adequacy rather than remembering one drug name.
manualAuthorGate.singleDefensibleBestAnswer: CAPOX is an evidence-supported offered adjuvant regimen in this fit R0 D2 stage III setting.
manualAuthorGate.counterfactual: Change D2/clear margins to an inadequate nodal dissection or R1 margin: a chemoradiation discussion becomes reasonable. Change chronology to initiation before surgery: contemporary perioperative immunotherapy evidence becomes relevant.
deletionTest: Upfront chronology distinguishes adjuvant from perioperative evidence.
D2 and clear margins determine the radiation comparison.
Functional recovery, renal function and neuropathy inform CAPOX feasibility; stage III establishes adjuvant need.
manualAuthorGate.sequenceReview: Standalone outside-hospital chart review. The ESD case does not become a fictional stage-III progression or an unsupported T1N2 adjuvant example.
manualAuthorGate.repairAndRecheck: Abandoned an ESD-to-T1N2 companion after finding a source limitation for that subgroup. Created this separate stage III case and rechecked the actual postoperative evidence; no FLOT-versus-durvalumab preference is silently inferred.

editorialDisposition.preservation: Exact reviewed artifacts preserved without any wording, profile, exhibit, option, feedback, node-order or rubric change.

fairness.issue: Among the offered choices, CAPOX is defensible after upfront clear-margin D2 resection of stage III disease in this recovered patient. The extent of dissection and absence of preoperative treatment make the radiation and perioperative-treatment extrapolation errors consequential.
fairness.disposition: Exact reviewed artifacts preserved without any wording, profile, exhibit, option, feedback, node-order or rubric change.

fairness.issue: Retained mismatch-repair proteins, renal function and neuropathy assessment address relevant treatment modifiers. The question supplies final stage rather than asking the learner to reconstruct it from an unspecified positive-node count; that is fair for this management objective.
fairness.disposition: Exact reviewed artifacts preserved without any wording, profile, exhibit, option, feedback, node-order or rubric change.

fairness.issue: The repeated CAPOX component does not uniquely identify the key: deciding whether to add nivolumab still requires knowledge. All options are comparably specific postoperative regimens.
fairness.disposition: Exact reviewed artifacts preserved without any wording, profile, exhibit, option, feedback, node-order or rubric change.

fairness.issue: Self-contained and high yield. No confident inaccuracy identified, but the time-sensitive immunotherapy/adjuvant boundary has not been freshly verified under the no-network constraint; editorial PASS is not clinical approval.

decisionNodes.stem: Which initial tumor-treatment plan best fits {patientName}'s gastric-mass records?

answerChoices.label: Preoperative imatinib with resection reassessment
answerChoices.rationale: The genotype supports imatinib responsiveness, and the anatomy gives shrinkage a consequential operative purpose. The combination supports a neoadjuvant plan rather than treatment from size alone.

answerChoices.label: Primary gastrectomy with margin-negative resection
answerChoices.rationale: Primary surgery treats the local disease but accepts the represented total-gastrectomy extent before exploring genotype-responsive reduction of that morbidity.

answerChoices.label: Preoperative avapritinib with resection reassessment
answerChoices.rationale: This substitutes a drug associated with another molecular subgroup for an imatinib-responsive KIT exon 11 tumor. Routine preoperative avapritinib is not established here.

decisionNodes.explanation: The molecular result and operative cost must both matter. KIT exon 11 supports imatinib responsiveness, while the cardia involvement gives response a reason to precede resection. Reassess the operation after treatment rather than assuming that every large GIST or every kinase inhibitor has the same pathway.

exhibit.caption: Original constructed teaching record; fictional patient observations

items.label: Core pathology and sequencing
items.value: Spindle-cell tumor with diffuse DOG1 and CD117 staining; sequencing identifies a KIT exon 11 deletion.

items.label: Operative anatomy
items.value: The mass encircles the cardia. The current margin-negative resection plan requires total gastrectomy; reducing the interface could allow a more limited gastric resection.

items.label: Clinical extent
items.value: No metastatic disease, active bleeding or obstruction is present.

decisionNodes.stem: Which drug plan best fits {patientName}'s first gastric-GIST response assessment?

answerChoices.label: Continue the current imatinib regimen
answerChoices.rationale: The attenuation and enhancement changes, absence of a new viable-appearing nodule, and clinical improvement support treatment effect despite the modest diameter increase.

answerChoices.label: Escalate the current imatinib regimen
answerChoices.rationale: The supplied pattern does not establish inadequate tumor suppression requiring dose escalation. Diameter change must be interpreted with density and clinical findings.

answerChoices.label: Replace imatinib with sunitinib
answerChoices.rationale: A second-line switch is premature when the integrated record supports response and no intolerance is present.

decisionNodes.explanation: Targeted GIST responses can reduce attenuation before the tumor shrinks. The matched protocol, lower attenuation, loss of enhancing tissue and improved symptoms argue against calling this imatinib failure from diameter alone. Continue the current regimen while following the planned response assessment.

question.stem: Which next tissue-acquisition procedure best fits {patientName}'s gastric-wall findings and the need for tumor classification and sequencing?

exhibit.caption: Original constructed teaching record; fictional patient observations

items.label: Endoscopy and submitted specimen
items.value: The mucosal surface over the cardia bulge is smooth. The forceps specimen contains gastric glands and lamina propria; no muscular tissue is present.

items.label: EUS images
items.value: An 8-cm mass is continuous with the fourth gastric-wall layer. Its enhancing solid portion lies against the luminal wall; the outer component contains a large fluid-filled region.

items.label: CT and surgical review
items.value: The anterior skin-to-solid-tumor trajectory crosses the transverse colon. The proposed diagnostic wedge would cross the gastroesophageal junction and require gastric reconstruction. No distant lesion is identified.

answerChoices.label: EUS-guided core biopsy of the solid component
answerChoices.rationale: The submitted mucosa does not represent the fourth-layer mass. EUS can target its solid component through the adjacent gastric wall and obtain tissue for classification and molecular testing without committing to a reconstructive resection.

answerChoices.label: CT-guided core biopsy of the solid component
answerChoices.rationale: Percutaneous core biopsy is a legitimate alternative for some GISTs, but the represented direct trajectory crosses colon while the solid target borders the gastric lumen. This anatomy favors EUS; percutaneous biopsy is not categorically prohibited.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: Percutaneous core biopsy is a legitimate alternative for some GISTs, but the represented direct trajectory crosses colon while the solid target borders the gastric lumen. This anatomy favors EUS; percutaneous biopsy is not categorically prohibited.

answerChoices.label: Laparoscopic wedge excision of the wall mass
answerChoices.rationale: Excision would obtain diagnostic tissue but here entails gastroesophageal-junction reconstruction before the tumor type is known. Representative needle tissue can determine whether such an operation is appropriate.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: Excision would obtain diagnostic tissue but here entails gastroesophageal-junction reconstruction before the tumor type is known. Representative needle tissue can determine whether such an operation is appropriate.

question.explanation: The benign mucosal sample and the fourth-layer mass describe different compartments. After recognizing that mismatch, compare routes to solid tumor rather than repeat superficial sampling or use a cystic component. The represented luminal relationship, transcolonic percutaneous trajectory and reconstructive cost of excision favor EUS-guided core tissue. Archived tissue from a different specimen must not substitute merely because a report is attached to the referral.

manualAuthorGate.coverTheKey: No report declares the sample inadequate or the lesion reachable. Raw specimen layers and route geometry must be compared with the target before choosing among three tissue procedures.
manualAuthorGate.sameDecisionStageAndCategory: All choices obtain representative tumor tissue now; none is a repeated unchanged forceps biopsy or an unrelated staging test.
reasoningSteps: Infer that glands and lamina propria do not classify a fourth-layer mass even though the surface biopsy is benign.
Compare access to solid tumor and the cost of diagnostic excision; choose EUS core in this represented anatomy.
manualAuthorGate.closestError: CT-guided core is a credible technique but ignores the colon on the represented skin-to-solid-target trajectory.
manualAuthorGate.decidingObservation: Solid tumor borders the luminal wall, while colon lies on the direct percutaneous trajectory and a wedge crosses the gastroesophageal junction.
manualAuthorGate.consequence: Obtain classifying and sequenceable tumor tissue without an avoidable transcolonic approach or reconstructive diagnostic excision.
manualAuthorGate.residentDifficulty: Moderate after repair: compartment interpretation followed by access selection; not labeled hard merely because EUS is specialized.
manualAuthorGate.singleDefensibleBestAnswer: EUS core is the best offered route for these observations. No universal EUS-over-percutaneous rule or invented assay-adequacy threshold is asserted.
manualAuthorGate.counterfactual: With solid tumor beyond EUS reach and a safe skin trajectory, CT-guided core could become the preferred offered procedure.
deletionTest: Delete the specimen layers and the reason a benign report fails to classify the mass is lost.
Delete route geometry and the EUS-versus-percutaneous preference is less discriminating; no prediction of treatment benefit is supplied.
manualAuthorGate.sequenceReview: Self-contained singleton; no prior explanation announces preoperative imatinib and no later genotype is exposed.
manualAuthorGate.repairAndRecheck: One review response removed feasibility language and the weak unchanged-forceps foil, retained neutral anatomy, and incorporated provenance as unscored feedback. Re-review remains required.

editorialDisposition.clarity: Raw glands/lamina propria versus fourth-wall-layer findings replace an explicit inadequacy conclusion. No assay threshold is invented.
editorialDisposition.cues: Removed reachable-from-lumen permission wording and preoperative-drug framing. Used solid/cystic anatomy, a represented transcolonic trajectory and reconstructive excision cost instead of unchanged forceps sampling.
editorialDisposition.fairness: All options obtain tumor tissue. CT-guided core remains a legitimate nearest competitor in suitable anatomy; feedback states its counterfactual rather than falsely prohibiting it. No downstream treatment result is exposed.
editorialDisposition.suggestions: Separated the node from the treatment chain. The rubric requires specimen-compartment interpretation followed by route choice. The low-yield archive principle is non-scored feedback only.

choices.label: Preoperative imatinib with resection reassessment
choices.rationale: The genotype supports imatinib responsiveness, and the anatomy gives shrinkage a consequential operative purpose. The combination supports a neoadjuvant plan rather than treatment from size alone.
choices.temptation: Combine predictive molecular evidence with a patient-specific operative consequence.
choices.counterfactual: A similarly genotyped peripheral lesion removable by a small wedge would favor primary surgery rather than automatically adding preoperative treatment.

choices.rationale: Primary surgery treats the local disease but accepts the represented total-gastrectomy extent before exploring genotype-responsive reduction of that morbidity.
choices.temptation: Apply the usual localized-GIST surgery rule without accounting for the particular cardia anatomy.
choices.counterfactual: A straightforward limited resection, an urgent complication or an imatinib-resistant genotype can change the initial plan.

choices.label: Preoperative avapritinib with resection reassessment
choices.rationale: This substitutes a drug associated with another molecular subgroup for an imatinib-responsive KIT exon 11 tumor. Routine preoperative avapritinib is not established here.
choices.temptation: Treat all kinase-driven GIST as interchangeable targeted-therapy candidates.
choices.counterfactual: PDGFRA D842V with unresectable or metastatic disease supports avapritinib; that is a different genotype and indication.

manualAuthorGate.coverTheKey: The record gives cardia encirclement and the proposed operation without predicting shrinkage, organ preservation or a preferred treatment sequence. Genotype and operative morbidity must both inform the plan.
manualAuthorGate.sameDecisionStageAndCategory: Three initial local-tumor treatment strategies.
reasoningSteps: Interpret the diagnostic phenotype and KIT exon 11 deletion as an imatinib-responsive GIST.
Use the cardia-related total-gastrectomy consequence to favor preoperative response before resection.
manualAuthorGate.closestError: Proceed to total gastrectomy because the disease is localized and technically removable.
manualAuthorGate.decidingObservation: KIT exon 11 supplies drug sensitivity; cardia encirclement with proposed total gastrectomy supplies a consequential reason to consider treatment before surgery.
manualAuthorGate.consequence: The wrong sequence can impose avoidable gastric loss or expose the patient to an unsuitable drug.
manualAuthorGate.residentDifficulty: Moderate to hard PGY-2/3 prediction from genotype versus operability, not the source's former sensitivity label.
manualAuthorGate.singleDefensibleBestAnswer: Among these options, preoperative imatinib addresses both a responsive driver and the represented avoidable surgical extent.
manualAuthorGate.counterfactual: Change cardia encirclement to a peripheral wedge-resectable lesion: primary surgery becomes preferable. Change to metastatic D842V: avapritinib becomes the appropriate offered drug in that revised indication.
deletionTest: Without genotype, imatinib responsiveness is not established and empiric treatment is unsafe.
Without the morbid operative anatomy, a readily resectable localized GIST could favor primary surgery; size alone does not dictate neoadjuvant therapy.
manualAuthorGate.sequenceReview: Self-contained singleton repeats pathology and extent; the prior tissue-acquisition item and its treatment-scaffolding feedback are absent.
manualAuthorGate.repairAndRecheck: One review response removed the explicit organ-preservation prediction and split the returned chain. The already defensible genotype-by-anatomy decision remains; independent re-review is pending.

editorialDisposition.clarity: Task, histology, genotype and extent are self-contained at initial treatment planning.

editorialDisposition.fairness: The original defensible imatinib/primary surgery/avapritinib comparison and necessary no-emergency findings remain. No prior tissue-node feedback announces drugs before surgery.
editorialDisposition.suggestions: Converted to a singleton. The two necessary inputs remain genotype-specific sensitivity and the operative cost that gives neoadjuvant treatment a consequential purpose.

case.learningSummary: Interpret a benign sample in relation to what it contains. This specimen describes superficial mucosa, while the treatment question concerns a deeper wall mass. Representative EUS-guided core tissue and molecular evaluation fit the selected pretreatment pathway; not every resectable GIST needs this sequence. The molecular result and operative cost must both matter. KIT exon 11 supports imatinib responsiveness, while the cardia involvement gives response a reason to precede resection. Reassess the operation after treatment rather than assuming that every large GIST or every kinase inhibitor has the same pathway. Targeted GIST responses can reduce attenuation before the tumor shrinks. The matched protocol, lower attenuation, loss of enhancing tissue and improved symptoms argue against calling this imatinib failure from diameter alone. Continue the current regimen while following the planned response assessment.

exhibit.caption: Original constructed teaching record; fictional patient observations

items.label: Pretreatment tissue and plan
items.value: Core biopsy showed DOG1-positive GIST with a KIT exon 11 deletion. The cardia location prompted preoperative imatinib before the proposed total gastrectomy.

items.label: Matched contrast CT measurements
items.value: The same acquisition phase and lesion region were used. Maximum diameter changed from 8.0 to 10.8 cm; mean attenuation changed from 72 to 34 HU.

items.label: Other imaging observations
items.value: No new enhancing intratumoral nodule or additional lesion is present. There is no internal high-attenuation blood product or peritumoral fluid.

answerChoices.label: Continue the current imatinib regimen
answerChoices.rationale: A substantial fall in attenuation on comparable scans can represent GIST response despite increased size. The lack of a new enhancing nodule or additional lesion supports continuing while the specialist team follows the response, rather than declaring resistance from diameter alone.

answerChoices.label: Escalate the current imatinib regimen
answerChoices.rationale: Size has increased, but the density change is a competing treatment-effect signal. Escalation for presumed resistance should not follow a diameter-only progression call before integrated GIST response review.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: Size has increased, but the density change is a competing treatment-effect signal. Escalation for presumed resistance should not follow a diameter-only progression call before integrated GIST response review.

answerChoices.label: Replace imatinib with sunitinib
answerChoices.rationale: A second-line drug presumes failure or intolerance. The supplied discordant scan does not establish failure, and dose-limiting toxicity is absent.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: A second-line drug presumes failure or intolerance. The supplied discordant scan does not establish failure, and dose-limiting toxicity is absent.

question.explanation: The larger diameter cannot be ignored, but it cannot be interpreted alone. On matched contrast imaging, the marked attenuation decrease without a new enhancing nodule can reflect imatinib effect even as a GIST enlarges. Continue the current regimen with specialist response review rather than escalate or switch on size alone. This is not a claim that every enlarging low-density lesion is responding.

choices.label: Continue the current imatinib regimen
choices.rationale: A substantial fall in attenuation on comparable scans can represent GIST response despite increased size. The lack of a new enhancing nodule or additional lesion supports continuing while the specialist team follows the response, rather than declaring resistance from diameter alone.
choices.temptation: Interpret the discordant measurements before selecting a treatment line.
choices.counterfactual: New enhancing viable tumor or additional progressive sites would require reassessment for true progression rather than continuation on the basis of low mean density alone.

choices.label: Escalate the current imatinib regimen
choices.rationale: Size has increased, but the density change is a competing treatment-effect signal. Escalation for presumed resistance should not follow a diameter-only progression call before integrated GIST response review.
choices.temptation: Apply a size-only solid-tumor progression rule to a targeted GIST response.
choices.counterfactual: Confirmed progression after adherence, interactions and imaging have been reviewed can make dose escalation a specialist option in appropriate disease.

choices.label: Replace imatinib with sunitinib
choices.rationale: A second-line drug presumes failure or intolerance. The supplied discordant scan does not establish failure, and dose-limiting toxicity is absent.
choices.temptation: Treat any diameter increase as sufficient evidence to abandon first-line therapy.
choices.counterfactual: Confirmed imatinib resistance or relevant intolerance would make second-line treatment a different decision.

manualAuthorGate.coverTheKey: Neither improved symptoms nor a qualitative radiology response conclusion is supplied. A large diameter increase competes with the raw matched-protocol attenuation decrease.
manualAuthorGate.sameDecisionStageAndCategory: Three current systemic-treatment plans compare continuation, dose escalation and line change after the same first response assessment.
reasoningSteps: Interpret increased diameter together with lower attenuation and absence of new enhancing tumor on comparable scans.
Distinguish possible targeted-treatment response from established failure before deciding whether to continue or change treatment.
manualAuthorGate.closestError: Escalating imatinib after reading only the increased diameter is the nearest credible error; the size change is no longer a small subthreshold distraction.
manualAuthorGate.decidingObservation: Attenuation falls from 72 to 34 HU using the same acquisition phase and lesion region, without a new enhancing nodule or additional lesion.
manualAuthorGate.consequence: Avoid prematurely abandoning or escalating effective treatment on a size-only progression interpretation.
manualAuthorGate.residentDifficulty: Moderate-to-hard intended response interpretation, pending independent review; no numeric response cutoff is invented or scored.
manualAuthorGate.singleDefensibleBestAnswer: Continue is the best offered drug plan while expert response assessment proceeds. An additional scan or PET is not forced against drug decisions, and no unsupported universal response diagnosis is made.
manualAuthorGate.counterfactual: A new enhancing intratumoral nodule or additional progressive sites would defeat the simple response interpretation and prompt resistance evaluation.
deletionTest: Hide attenuation and the large diameter increase makes progression and escalation credible; density is necessary to the scored choice.
Remove symptom improvement entirely: the item still depends on imaging interpretation, not redundant clinical-success language.
manualAuthorGate.sequenceReview: Self-contained singleton supplies tumor type, genotype and current treatment; earlier feedback cannot supply the attenuation interpretation.
manualAuthorGate.repairAndRecheck: One response replaced the 7.5% size change with a consequential constructed enlargement, removed symptom-success and qualitative-density cues, and retained matched acquisition plus progression checks. Re-review is pending.

editorialDisposition.clarity: Matched acquisition phase and lesion region remain explicit; no response cutoff or clinical probability is invented.
editorialDisposition.cues: Removed improved satiety/intake and qualitative low-attenuation response wording. Constructed diameter is now 8.0 to 10.8 cm with attenuation 72 to 34 HU; the original 7.5% size change no longer makes density irrelevant.
editorialDisposition.fairness: Retained absence of a new enhancing nodule/additional lesion and dose-limiting toxicity, as necessary for a fair response-versus-failure plan. No symptoms independently establish success. Expert integrated review remains required.
editorialDisposition.suggestions: Deletion check now changes the comparison: hiding density makes the substantial enlargement support a plausible failure interpretation. The rubric names dose escalation as the nearest error and new enhancing tumor as the counterfactual.
