revisedProposals.task: Which systemic-treatment plan best fits {patientName}'s first response assessment for gastric GIST?

exhibit.caption: Original constructed teaching record; fictional patient observations

items.label: Pretreatment tissue and plan
items.value: Core biopsy showed DOG1-positive GIST with a KIT exon 11 deletion. The cardia location prompted preoperative imatinib before the proposed total gastrectomy.

items.label: Matched contrast CT measurements
items.value: The same acquisition phase and lesion region were used. Maximum diameter changed from 8.0 to 10.8 cm; mean attenuation changed from 72 to 34 HU.

items.label: Other imaging observations
items.value: No new enhancing intratumoral nodule or additional lesion is present. There is no internal high-attenuation blood product or peritumoral fluid.

choices.label: Continue the current imatinib regimen
choices.rationale: A substantial fall in attenuation on comparable scans can represent GIST response despite increased size. The lack of a new enhancing nodule or additional lesion supports continuing while the specialist team follows the response, rather than declaring resistance from diameter alone.
choices.temptation: Interpret the discordant measurements before selecting a treatment line.
choices.counterfactual: New enhancing viable tumor or additional progressive sites would require reassessment for true progression rather than continuation on the basis of low mean density alone.

choices.label: Escalate the current imatinib regimen
choices.rationale: Size has increased, but the density change is a competing treatment-effect signal. Escalation for presumed resistance should not follow a diameter-only progression call before integrated GIST response review.
choices.temptation: Apply a size-only solid-tumor progression rule to a targeted GIST response.
choices.counterfactual: Confirmed progression after adherence, interactions and imaging have been reviewed can make dose escalation a specialist option in appropriate disease.

choices.label: Replace imatinib with sunitinib
choices.rationale: A second-line drug presumes failure or intolerance. The supplied discordant scan does not establish failure, and dose-limiting toxicity is absent.
choices.temptation: Treat any diameter increase as sufficient evidence to abandon first-line therapy.
choices.counterfactual: Confirmed imatinib resistance or relevant intolerance would make second-line treatment a different decision.

revisedProposals.explanation: The larger diameter cannot be ignored, but it cannot be interpreted alone. On matched contrast imaging, the marked attenuation decrease without a new enhancing nodule can reflect imatinib effect even as a GIST enlarges. Continue the current regimen with specialist response review rather than escalate or switch on size alone. This is not a claim that every enlarging low-density lesion is responding.

manualAuthorGate.coverTheKey: Neither improved symptoms nor a qualitative radiology response conclusion is supplied. A large diameter increase competes with the raw matched-protocol attenuation decrease.
manualAuthorGate.sameDecisionStageAndCategory: Three current systemic-treatment plans compare continuation, dose escalation and line change after the same first response assessment.
reasoningSteps: Interpret increased diameter together with lower attenuation and absence of new enhancing tumor on comparable scans.
Distinguish possible targeted-treatment response from established failure before deciding whether to continue or change treatment.
manualAuthorGate.closestError: Escalating imatinib after reading only the increased diameter is the nearest credible error; the size change is no longer a small subthreshold distraction.
manualAuthorGate.decidingObservation: Attenuation falls from 72 to 34 HU using the same acquisition phase and lesion region, without a new enhancing nodule or additional lesion.
manualAuthorGate.consequence: Avoid prematurely abandoning or escalating effective treatment on a size-only progression interpretation.
manualAuthorGate.residentDifficulty: Moderate-to-hard intended response interpretation, pending independent review; no numeric response cutoff is invented or scored.
manualAuthorGate.singleDefensibleBestAnswer: Continue is the best offered drug plan while expert response assessment proceeds. An additional scan or PET is not forced against drug decisions, and no unsupported universal response diagnosis is made.
manualAuthorGate.counterfactual: A new enhancing intratumoral nodule or additional progressive sites would defeat the simple response interpretation and prompt resistance evaluation.
deletionTest: Hide attenuation and the large diameter increase makes progression and escalation credible; density is necessary to the scored choice.
Remove symptom improvement entirely: the item still depends on imaging interpretation, not redundant clinical-success language.
manualAuthorGate.sequenceReview: Self-contained singleton supplies tumor type, genotype and current treatment; earlier feedback cannot supply the attenuation interpretation.
manualAuthorGate.repairAndRecheck: One response replaced the 7.5% size change with a consequential constructed enlargement, removed symptom-success and qualitative-density cues, and retained matched acquisition plus progression checks. Re-review is pending.

revisedProposals.objective: Maintain effective imatinib after response and removal of metastatic gastric GIST rather than apply a finite-adjuvant stopping rule.
revisedProposals.task: Which ongoing systemic-treatment plan best fits {patientName}'s gastric-GIST treatment records?

exhibit.caption: Original constructed teaching record; fictional patient observations

items.label: Original disease
items.value: A gastric GIST and biopsy-confirmed liver metastasis both carried a KIT exon 11 alteration.

items.label: Treatment and operation
items.value: Both sites regressed during imatinib. The residual gastric and liver lesions were then completely removed without rupture.

items.label: Current follow-up
items.value: CT shows no visible tumor. She continues imatinib with good tolerance and no progression; she asks about stopping because the scans are clear.

choices.label: Continue imatinib during scan-negative follow-up
choices.rationale: The liver biopsy established metastatic GIST before treatment. Resection and a clear current scan do not convert ongoing effective metastatic therapy into a finite adjuvant course; continue while effective and tolerated.
choices.temptation: Use the original disease state as well as the current scan.
choices.counterfactual: A completely resected localized primary without metastasis would instead raise a risk- and genotype-dependent finite adjuvant decision.

choices.label: Set an adjuvant-course endpoint and then stop imatinib
choices.rationale: This applies a finite localized-adjuvant framework to previously biopsy-proven metastatic disease. The original liver metastasis remains consequential after all visible sites have been removed.
choices.temptation: Reclassify postoperative absence of visible tumor as localized adjuvant treatment.
choices.counterfactual: If the original disease had been confined to a completely resected primary, a finite evidence-supported adjuvant course could be appropriate for a sensitive high-risk tumor.

choices.label: Stop imatinib now and restart at measurable recurrence
choices.rationale: A monitored stop-and-restart policy is not equivalent to maintaining effective treatment in metastatic GIST. A current clear scan does not establish that interruption is safe.
choices.temptation: Treat surveillance and later re-treatment as substitutes for suppressing known metastatic disease continuously.
choices.counterfactual: Relevant intolerance would require a toxicity-driven treatment reassessment; it is absent here and is not a scan-clearance stopping rule.

revisedProposals.explanation: Interpret the pretreatment liver biopsy before assigning the current treatment phase. This remains previously metastatic GIST despite complete resection and clear scans. Effective, tolerated imatinib continues; neither a finite localized-adjuvant endpoint nor scan-triggered stop-and-restart follows from radiographic clearance.

manualAuthorGate.coverTheKey: The neutral task does not name imatinib. All three choices are imatinib-duration policies; tolerability no longer disposes of a mismatched line-switch option.
manualAuthorGate.sameDecisionStageAndCategory: Three ongoing-treatment policies differ in continuation, a finite adjuvant endpoint, or interruption until measurable recurrence.
reasoningSteps: Reconcile current radiographic clearance with the original biopsy-proven metastatic distribution.
Apply metastatic suppression rather than localized-adjuvant completion logic to the ongoing drug plan.
manualAuthorGate.closestError: Applying a finite adjuvant endpoint after complete metastasectomy is the nearest error, distinct from stopping immediately because the present scan is clear.
manualAuthorGate.decidingObservation: The original liver lesion was biopsy-confirmed metastatic GIST and the same drug remains effective and tolerated.
manualAuthorGate.consequence: Routine interruption can permit progression despite apparent remission.
manualAuthorGate.residentDifficulty: Moderate to hard PGY-2/3 prediction from treatment-intent and current-versus-historical disease-state confusion.
manualAuthorGate.singleDefensibleBestAnswer: Continue imatinib among the offered choices because the disease was metastatic and neither failure nor intolerance justifies changing therapy.
manualAuthorGate.counterfactual: Without an original metastatic site, completely resected localized high-risk sensitive GIST could warrant a finite adjuvant course; intolerance would require a different reassessment rather than a clearance-based stop.
deletionTest: Original metastatic tissue provenance prevents a benign liver lesion from being misread as spread.
Resection and clear CT make stopping genuinely tempting.
Current response and tolerance distinguish a continuation decision from drug failure management.
manualAuthorGate.sequenceReview: Self-contained singleton preserves original biopsy-proven metastasis, operative clearance and tolerability; no prerequisite case supplies its disease-phase conclusion.
manualAuthorGate.repairAndRecheck: One response neutralized the task and replaced the disposable sunitinib foil with a finite-adjuvant policy. No arbitrary stopping interval or new duration rule was introduced; re-review is pending.

revisedProposals.objective: Select a representative biopsy site when a new gastric-region lesion behaves differently from previously sampled MALT lymphoma.
revisedProposals.currentUpdate: The clinic reviews new outside imaging alongside a recent endoscopy report.
revisedProposals.task: Which tissue-acquisition plan should be arranged next for {patientName} before choosing treatment for the new gastric-region disease?

exhibit.caption: Original constructed teaching record; fictional patient observations

items.label: History and recent endoscopy
items.value: Gastric MALT lymphoma previously regressed after H. pylori eradication. New forceps samples from the old antral scar show small CD20-positive lymphocytes and lymphoepithelial lesions, without sheets of large cells.

items.label: Interval CT and laboratory results
items.value: A separate posterior gastric/perigastric mass has enlarged from 1.8 to 5.2 cm across the two recent scans. LDH is now 720 U/L (laboratory upper limit 250 U/L); the blood counts are normal.

items.label: PET/CT and endoscopic location map
items.value: The posterior mass has much greater FDG uptake than the old antral scar. It lies outside the mucosal biopsy sites and abuts the posterior gastric wall. No peripheral node is available for sampling.

choices.label: EUS-guided core biopsy of the posterior mass
choices.rationale: The recent small-cell mucosal sample represents the old site, not the rapidly enlarging metabolically discordant mass. Obtain representative tissue from the new lesion to evaluate a changed lymphoma component before selecting treatment; FDG uptake alone does not prove transformation.
choices.temptation: Reconcile which site was sampled with which site changed.
choices.counterfactual: If representative tissue from the changing mass had already established its histology, repeating acquisition would not answer a remaining staging question.

choices.label: Repeat forceps biopsies of the antral scar
choices.rationale: The scar biopsy can describe residual MALT at that site but does not classify the separate mass. Repeating the same old-site acquisition leaves the consequential spatial and biologic discrepancy unresolved.
choices.temptation: Let a recent low-grade gastric result stand for all current gastric-region disease.
choices.counterfactual: If the uncertain progressive lesion were mucosal and located in that scar, directed repeat endoscopic sampling could be representative.

choices.label: Iliac-crest marrow aspirate and trephine biopsy
choices.rationale: Marrow assessment may answer selected staging questions, but it does not sample the lesion responsible for the current discrepancy. Normal blood counts do not prove absence of marrow disease; the immediate need is the new mass's histology.
choices.temptation: Substitute another lymphoma staging specimen for tissue from the changing focal lesion.
choices.counterfactual: A specific marrow or cytopenia question could justify marrow sampling, but would not replace biopsy of a discordant mass suspected of a changed component.

revisedProposals.explanation: A low-grade result from the old mucosal scar cannot classify a different rapidly enlarging, more FDG-avid mass. The clinical and imaging discrepancy raises concern for a changed component, but requires histologic confirmation. Use the PET/location map to obtain representative tissue from that mass rather than repeat the old scar or substitute a staging specimen.

manualAuthorGate.coverTheKey: No expert report supplies transformation or declares current tissue inadequate. The learner must compare the actual sampled site, small-cell findings and separate changing lesion.
manualAuthorGate.sameDecisionStageAndCategory: All three options are specific tissue-acquisition plans before treatment selection; no drug or unrelated local staging procedure is a category outlier.
reasoningSteps: Interpret discordant growth, LDH and FDG avidity despite small-cell histology from a different gastric site as an unresolved possible changed component.
Choose tissue from the changing mass rather than repeat a nonrepresentative old site or substitute marrow staging.
manualAuthorGate.closestError: Repeat old-scar endoscopy is a credible gastric-lymphoma acquisition habit but samples the already described low-grade compartment again.
manualAuthorGate.decidingObservation: The rapidly enlarging FDG-avid posterior mass lies outside the antral mucosal biopsy sites; no specimen yet classifies that mass.
manualAuthorGate.consequence: Avoid selecting a low-grade or aggressive treatment pathway without representative confirmation of the new lesion.
manualAuthorGate.residentDifficulty: Moderate-to-hard intended spatial/specimen reasoning, pending review. PET avidity is not treated as a diagnostic threshold or proof of transformation.
manualAuthorGate.singleDefensibleBestAnswer: The mass's location against the gastric wall supports targeted EUS core as the best offered representative acquisition; the other specimens do not resolve its histology.
manualAuthorGate.counterfactual: A changing mucosal lesion actually located within the sampled antral scar would support directed repeat endoscopic biopsy there; already established mass histology would move the task to staging or treatment.
deletionTest: Delete the sampled-site map and repeat scar biopsy may look equally representative, making the item unfair.
Delete the growth/LDH/avidity discrepancy and the urgency of obtaining new mass histology is weakened; no cutoff is needed.
manualAuthorGate.sequenceReview: Standalone new meaning: the previous PET-staging node is archived, not a prerequisite. No lymphoma-treatment explanation or diagnosis is revealed first.
manualAuthorGate.repairAndRecheck: One response replaced direct PET recall with an unresolved site-specific tissue problem, removed vague H. pylori wording and the frozen-version sentence, and created a distinct concept identity. Re-review is pending.

revisedProposals.objective: Distinguish an anthracycline-free lymphoma regimen from simple dose attenuation when cardiac dysfunction constrains treatment of gastric large-B-cell lymphoma.
revisedProposals.currentUpdate: The clinic reviews outside hematopathology and pretreatment assessment for a hematology planning visit.
revisedProposals.task: Which initial systemic regimen best fits {patientName}'s gastric diffuse large-B-cell lymphoma and pretreatment findings among the options offered?

exhibit.caption: Original constructed teaching record; fictional patient observations

items.label: Lymphoma record
items.value: Gastric biopsies establish CD20-positive diffuse large-B-cell lymphoma. Systemic treatment with curative intent is planned. There is no perforation, ongoing hemorrhage or obstruction.

items.label: Functional assessment
items.value: She is independently active, walks without assistance and has preserved renal and hepatic function. There is no general frailty limiting combination treatment.

items.label: Cardiac assessment
items.value: Longstanding ischemic cardiomyopathy predates the lymphoma. Repeat echocardiography after cardiac optimization shows left ventricular ejection fraction 30%; previous examinations show similar values.

choices.label: R-CEOP combination immunochemotherapy
choices.rationale: Persistent marked systolic dysfunction makes doxorubicin exposure the limiting issue despite preserved general function. R-CEOP substitutes etoposide for doxorubicin and is a guideline-supported offered option for anthracycline-ineligible large-B-cell lymphoma, with hematology and cardio-oncology review.
choices.temptation: Distinguish organ-specific contraindication from a need to reduce every drug because of frailty.
choices.counterfactual: With preserved cardiac function and no anthracycline contraindication, an anthracycline-containing first-line regimen could be preferred; R-CEOP is not claimed superior for all patients.

choices.label: R-CHOP combination immunochemotherapy
choices.rationale: R-CHOP includes doxorubicin. Otherwise good function does not remove the persistent severe systolic dysfunction that changes the appropriate drug backbone.
choices.temptation: Apply the usual aggressive-lymphoma regimen based on performance status while overlooking organ-specific cardiac risk.
choices.counterfactual: Preserved systolic function without a relevant anthracycline contraindication would make R-CHOP a defensible first-line option in an appropriate disease setting.

choices.label: R-mini-CHOP combination immunochemotherapy
choices.rationale: Dose-attenuated R-mini-CHOP retains doxorubicin; it does not remove the drug constrained by this cardiac assessment. The record supports a cardiac-specific substitution rather than treating an independently active 69-year-old as generally frail.
choices.temptation: Use dose attenuation as a universal solution to organ-specific anthracycline ineligibility.
choices.counterfactual: A suitable very elderly patient without this cardiac constraint may be considered for attenuated R-mini-CHOP; that different fitness problem is not represented here.

revisedProposals.explanation: The biopsy establishes the lymphoma family, but the regimen comparison turns on pretreatment fitness. Persistent severe systolic dysfunction changes whether doxorubicin belongs in the regimen; preserved independence does not cancel that constraint. R-CEOP is the supported offered anthracycline-free alternative. Simply reducing CHOP doses still exposes her to doxorubicin. Other specialist alternatives exist; this item does not rank them or prescribe doses or cycles.

manualAuthorGate.coverTheKey: All options treat aggressive B-cell lymphoma at the same phase. The exhibit reports raw repeat LVEF and functional observations without declaring anthracycline ineligibility.
manualAuthorGate.sameDecisionStageAndCategory: Three named initial combination immunochemotherapy regimens; no MALT-only radiation or epithelial-cancer operation is used as an easy disease-category foil.
reasoningSteps: Distinguish persistent severe organ-specific systolic dysfunction from age alone or general frailty in an independently active patient.
Choose a doxorubicin-free backbone rather than the usual or dose-attenuated doxorubicin-containing CHOP regimen.
manualAuthorGate.closestError: R-mini-CHOP is a credible attempt to accommodate fitness but retains the very anthracycline constrained by the repeated cardiac assessment.
manualAuthorGate.decidingObservation: Repeated LVEF is 30% despite cardiac optimization, while general independence and renal/hepatic function remain preserved.
manualAuthorGate.consequence: Discuss a curative-intent lymphoma plan without treating dose attenuation as removal of anthracycline cardiac exposure.
manualAuthorGate.residentDifficulty: Moderate intended regimen discrimination with a meaningful fitness modifier, pending independent review; no unsupported superiority claim or dose arithmetic.
manualAuthorGate.singleDefensibleBestAnswer: R-CEOP is supported among these choices. Other accepted anthracycline-ineligible regimens are deliberately not offered as competing equally defensible keys.
manualAuthorGate.counterfactual: Preserved cardiac function would restore an anthracycline-containing first-line option; general age-related vulnerability without cardiac ineligibility would raise a different attenuation question.
deletionTest: Hide the cardiac findings and R-CHOP becomes a defensible default; the new modifier changes the scored regimen.
Delete diagnosis and treatment intent and the regimen comparison lacks necessary context; no unnecessary PET result is used to pretend to add a step.
manualAuthorGate.sequenceReview: Self-contained singleton repeats diagnosis, treatment intent and complication screen. No preceding large-cell explanation rehearses the cardiac discriminator.
manualAuthorGate.repairAndRecheck: One response replaced cross-disease foils with lymphoma regimens and a source-verified cardiac constraint, removed unnecessary infection/stage detail, and created a distinct concept meaning. Re-review remains required.

questions.stem: Which additional staging procedure should be arranged for {patientName} before the proposed gastric-cancer treatment sequence?

exhibit.caption: Original constructed teaching record; fictional patient observations

items.label: Endoscopy and biopsy
items.value: Most of the gastric body is rigid and poorly distensible. Multiple biopsies contain poorly cohesive adenocarcinoma.

items.label: Contrast CT chest, abdomen and pelvis
items.value: Diffuse gastric-wall thickening reaches the surrounding fat. Several regional nodes are enlarged. No ascites, peritoneal nodule or distant organ lesion is identified.

answerChoices.label: Staging laparoscopy with peritoneal washings
answerChoices.rationale: The diffuse advanced pattern raises concern for disease that CT may not show on the peritoneal surface. Laparoscopic inspection and washings can alter the intended treatment sequence.

answerChoices.label: Endoscopic ultrasound with regional-node sampling
answerChoices.rationale: Regional depth and node information would not settle the consequential possibility of occult peritoneal spread in this advanced diffuse presentation.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: Regional depth and node information would not settle the consequential possibility of occult peritoneal spread in this advanced diffuse presentation.

answerChoices.label: Whole-body FDG PET/CT for distant staging
answerChoices.rationale: A metabolic survey does not replace direct peritoneal assessment and cytology in this selected high-risk pattern.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: A metabolic survey does not replace direct peritoneal assessment and cytology in this selected high-risk pattern.

questions.explanation: Diffuse advanced gastric involvement changes what a negative CT can establish. Laparoscopic peritoneal staging can uncover a treatment-changing distribution before the planned sequence; this is not a rule for every early gastric lesion.

questions.stem: Which treatment sequence should the clinic recommend discussing for {patientName}'s newly returned gastric-cancer staging findings?

exhibit.caption: Original constructed teaching record; fictional patient observations

items.label: Laparoscopic findings
items.value: No visible peritoneal deposit was seen. Washings were collected before manipulation of the primary tumor.

items.label: Cytology
items.value: Malignant epithelial cells with features concordant with the gastric primary are present.

items.label: Current clinical course
items.value: She continues oral intake and has no ongoing bleeding or obstruction.

answerChoices.label: Systemic treatment, then reassess resection candidacy
answerChoices.rationale: The positive washings establish clinically important spread despite an unrevealing visual survey. With this finding obtained before initial treatment, systemic treatment precedes reconsideration of surgery; subsequent clearance can change candidacy.

answerChoices.label: Upfront gastrectomy, then postoperative chemotherapy
answerChoices.rationale: This treats a pre-initial-treatment cytology result as if it were a finding discovered during an already undertaken gastrectomy. The chronology matters.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: This treats a pre-initial-treatment cytology result as if it were a finding discovered during an already undertaken gastrectomy. The chronology matters.

answerChoices.label: Gastric chemoradiation, then reassess resection candidacy
answerChoices.rationale: A stomach-focused treatment strategy does not address the demonstrated peritoneal distribution in the way a systemic-first plan does.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: A stomach-focused treatment strategy does not address the demonstrated peritoneal distribution in the way a systemic-first plan does.

questions.explanation: Positive washings and a negative visual survey are not equivalent staging results. Because cytology was obtained before initial treatment, discuss systemic therapy followed by reassessment rather than immediate gastrectomy. This does not assert that surgery can never become appropriate.

questions.stem: Which management plan should be discussed for {patientName} after review of the gastric endoscopic-resection specimen?

exhibit.caption: Original constructed teaching record; fictional patient observations

items.label: Endoscopic specimen
items.value: An 18-mm differentiated tubular adenocarcinoma was removed en bloc. It is confined to the mucosa, with no ulceration; lateral and deep margins are clear.

items.label: Additional sections
items.value: Separate clusters of epithelial tumor cells lie inside endothelial-lined lymphatic spaces beneath the lesion.

items.label: Staging and health
items.value: CT shows no enlarged regional node or distant lesion. She is independently active and has no major cardiopulmonary disease.

answerChoices.label: Gastrectomy with lymphadenectomy
answerChoices.rationale: The lymphatic tumor finding changes endoscopic curability. A clear scar and normal-size nodes do not eliminate the concern outside the endoscopically removed mucosal field.

answerChoices.label: Repeat endoscopic submucosal dissection
answerChoices.rationale: More scar resection does not address lymphatic involvement when the existing mucosal resection margins are already clear.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: More scar resection does not address lymphatic involvement when the existing mucosal resection margins are already clear.

answerChoices.label: Endoscopic and radiologic surveillance
answerChoices.rationale: Surveillance gives excessive weight to the small mucosal lesion, clear margins and CT node size while overlooking the lymphatic finding in a fit patient.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: Surveillance gives excessive weight to the small mucosal lesion, clear margins and CT node size while overlooking the lymphatic finding in a fit patient.

questions.explanation: Clear margins answer a local removal question. Tumor within lymphatic spaces changes the concern for disease beyond that field. In this fit patient, completion gastrectomy with lymphadenectomy is the supported discussion despite unrevealing CT nodes.

questions.stem: Which postoperative treatment should be discussed for {patientName}'s gastric cancer on the basis of the outside operative and pathology records?

exhibit.caption: Original constructed teaching record; fictional patient observations

items.label: Prior treatment
items.value: The outside hospital performed upfront gastrectomy; she received no preoperative drug treatment or radiotherapy.

items.label: Operation and pathology
items.value: D2 dissection is documented with clear gastric margins. The primary extends into subserosa, and regional nodes contain carcinoma; the final pathology stage is III.

items.label: Treatment assessment
items.value: Mismatch-repair proteins are retained. She has recovered oral intake, with preserved renal function and no function-limiting neuropathy.

answerChoices.label: Adjuvant CAPOX chemotherapy
answerChoices.rationale: Capecitabine and oxaliplatin are supported after curative D2 surgery for stage II/III disease. This is postoperative treatment after upfront surgery, not selection of a new perioperative regimen.

answerChoices.label: Adjuvant capecitabine chemoradiation
answerChoices.rationale: The completed R0 D2 record lacks the margin or inadequate-dissection boundary that would make a postoperative local-control strategy more compelling.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: The completed R0 D2 record lacks the margin or inadequate-dissection boundary that would make a postoperative local-control strategy more compelling.

answerChoices.label: Adjuvant CAPOX plus nivolumab
answerChoices.rationale: The adjuvant nivolumab trial after upfront D2 surgery did not establish added benefit. A newer perioperative immunotherapy approval is not interchangeable with this postoperative-only plan.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: The adjuvant nivolumab trial after upfront D2 surgery did not establish added benefit. A newer perioperative immunotherapy approval is not interchangeable with this postoperative-only plan.

questions.explanation: Match systemic treatment to the pathway that actually occurred. Stage III disease after upfront R0 D2 resection supports adjuvant CAPOX among these options. Adequate dissection and clear margins affect the radiation comparison; postoperative nivolumab is not established by perioperative immunotherapy results.

questions.stem: Which operation best fits {patientName}'s localized gastric tumor?

exhibit.caption: Original constructed teaching record; fictional patient observations

items.label: Biopsy
items.value: A spindle-cell tumor stains for DOG1 and CD117. KIT exon 11 is altered; SDHB expression is retained.

items.label: Contrast CT and EUS
items.value: A 3.2-cm mass projects from the greater-curvature side of the fundus. It does not encircle the cardia or contact an adjacent organ. No enlarged node or distant lesion is identified.

answerChoices.label: Full-thickness wedge gastrectomy
answerChoices.rationale: A limited resection can remove this peripheral conventional GIST with an intact capsule. Its lymphatic behavior differs from gastric adenocarcinoma, so routine D2 clearance is not required.

answerChoices.label: Total gastrectomy with D2 dissection
answerChoices.rationale: This applies an epithelial gastric-cancer operation and routine nodal strategy to a fundic mesenchymal tumor, with more gastric loss and no stated nodal indication.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: This applies an epithelial gastric-cancer operation and routine nodal strategy to a fundic mesenchymal tumor, with more gastric loss and no stated nodal indication.

answerChoices.label: Endoscopic submucosal enucleation
answerChoices.rationale: Shelling out a muscular-wall GIST does not provide the same assurance of complete excision with an intact capsule and appropriate wall clearance.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: Shelling out a muscular-wall GIST does not provide the same assurance of complete excision with an intact capsule and appropriate wall clearance.

questions.explanation: The biopsy establishes a conventional GIST pattern, and the peripheral fundic anatomy permits a local full-thickness excision. Preserve the capsule and obtain complete removal; do not substitute routine adenocarcinoma lymphadenectomy or shelling out the mass.

questions.stem: Which next management plan best fits {patientName}'s returned gastric-GIST resection records?

exhibit.caption: Original constructed teaching record; fictional patient observations

items.label: Operation
items.value: The mass was removed intact. No tumor spill, rupture or gross residual lesion was recorded.

items.label: Pathology
items.value: The 3.2-cm gastric GIST has two mitoses per 5 mm2. A microscopic focus reaches the inked gastric-wall edge.

items.label: Postoperative review
items.value: CT shows no residual mass. The postoperative remnant is narrowed near the cardia, and a wider resection would require completion total gastrectomy.

answerChoices.label: Scheduled CT tumor surveillance
answerChoices.rationale: A microscopic margin does not equal rupture or macroscopic residual tumor. Given the limited tumor risk features and major completion operation, review-based surveillance is the best offered plan rather than automatic resection or imatinib for the margin itself.

answerChoices.label: Completion total gastrectomy
answerChoices.rationale: The microscopic edge does not by itself establish benefit sufficient to justify the represented major gastric loss. Low-morbidity re-excision is a different discussion.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: The microscopic edge does not by itself establish benefit sufficient to justify the represented major gastric loss. Low-morbidity re-excision is a different discussion.

answerChoices.label: Adjuvant imatinib treatment
answerChoices.rationale: R1 status alone is not an adjuvant-imatinib criterion. The reported size, gastric site, low mitotic count and absence of rupture do not supply a high-risk indication in this case.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: R1 status alone is not an adjuvant-imatinib criterion. The reported size, gastric site, low mitotic count and absence of rupture do not supply a high-risk indication in this case.

questions.explanation: Read margin, gross residual tumor and rupture as separate findings. A microscopic edge in an otherwise intact, macroscopically complete resection does not independently require major completion surgery or adjuvant imatinib. The actual re-excision burden and tumor risk support surveillance among these choices.

questions.stem: Which postoperative plan should be discussed for {patientName}'s completely resected gastric tumor?

exhibit.caption: Original constructed teaching record; fictional patient observations

items.label: Resection record
items.value: The gastric GIST was removed intact with clear margins. No rupture, gross residual tumor or metastatic lesion was found.

items.label: Tumor pathology
items.value: The tumor measures 7 cm and has 12 mitoses per 5 mm2. Sequencing identifies PDGFRA exon 18 D842V.

answerChoices.label: CT surveillance after complete resection
answerChoices.rationale: The adverse risk features justify close sarcoma follow-up, but do not make an imatinib-resistant driver sensitive. Metastatic avapritinib activity does not establish routine adjuvant benefit after complete resection.

answerChoices.label: Adjuvant imatinib after complete resection
answerChoices.rationale: Size and mitotic activity cannot overcome primary D842V resistance. Adjuvant imatinib is not indicated for this molecular subtype.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: Size and mitotic activity cannot overcome primary D842V resistance. Adjuvant imatinib is not indicated for this molecular subtype.

answerChoices.label: Adjuvant avapritinib after complete resection
answerChoices.rationale: Selecting an active drug from the metastatic setting does not establish an adjuvant indication in a patient with complete local removal. A clinical trial is a separate discussion.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: Selecting an active drug from the metastatic setting does not establish an adjuvant indication in a patient with complete local removal. A clinical trial is a separate discussion.

questions.explanation: High recurrence risk is not a substitute for a supported adjuvant drug. D842V excludes routine adjuvant imatinib, and the established avapritinib indication concerns unresectable or metastatic disease. Use risk-based surveillance and sarcoma review rather than invent an adjuvant standard.

questions.stem: Which next tissue-acquisition procedure best fits {patientName}'s gastric-wall findings and the need for tumor classification and sequencing?

exhibit.caption: Original constructed teaching record; fictional patient observations

items.label: Endoscopy and submitted specimen
items.value: The mucosal surface over the cardia bulge is smooth. The forceps specimen contains gastric glands and lamina propria; no muscular tissue is present.

items.label: EUS images
items.value: An 8-cm mass is continuous with the fourth gastric-wall layer. Its enhancing solid portion lies against the luminal wall; the outer component contains a large fluid-filled region.

items.label: CT and surgical review
items.value: The anterior skin-to-solid-tumor trajectory crosses the transverse colon. The proposed diagnostic wedge would cross the gastroesophageal junction and require gastric reconstruction. No distant lesion is identified.

answerChoices.label: EUS-guided core biopsy of the solid component
answerChoices.rationale: The submitted mucosa does not represent the fourth-layer mass. EUS can target its solid component through the adjacent gastric wall and obtain tissue for classification and molecular testing without committing to a reconstructive resection.

answerChoices.label: CT-guided core biopsy of the solid component
answerChoices.rationale: Percutaneous core biopsy is a legitimate alternative for some GISTs, but the represented direct trajectory crosses colon while the solid target borders the gastric lumen. This anatomy favors EUS; percutaneous biopsy is not categorically prohibited.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: Percutaneous core biopsy is a legitimate alternative for some GISTs, but the represented direct trajectory crosses colon while the solid target borders the gastric lumen. This anatomy favors EUS; percutaneous biopsy is not categorically prohibited.

answerChoices.label: Laparoscopic wedge excision of the wall mass
answerChoices.rationale: Excision would obtain diagnostic tissue but here entails gastroesophageal-junction reconstruction before the tumor type is known. Representative needle tissue can determine whether such an operation is appropriate.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: Excision would obtain diagnostic tissue but here entails gastroesophageal-junction reconstruction before the tumor type is known. Representative needle tissue can determine whether such an operation is appropriate.

questions.explanation: The benign mucosal sample and the fourth-layer mass describe different compartments. After recognizing that mismatch, compare routes to solid tumor rather than repeat superficial sampling or use a cystic component. The represented luminal relationship, transcolonic percutaneous trajectory and reconstructive cost of excision favor EUS-guided core tissue. Archived tissue from a different specimen must not substitute merely because a report is attached to the referral.

questions.stem: Which initial tumor-treatment plan best fits {patientName}'s gastric-mass records?

exhibit.caption: Original constructed teaching record; fictional patient observations

items.label: Core pathology and sequencing
items.value: Spindle-cell tumor with diffuse DOG1 and CD117 staining; sequencing identifies a KIT exon 11 deletion.

items.label: Operative anatomy
items.value: The 8-cm mass encircles the cardia. The proposed margin-negative operation is total gastrectomy.

items.label: Clinical extent
items.value: No metastatic disease, active bleeding or obstruction is present.

answerChoices.label: Preoperative imatinib with resection reassessment
answerChoices.rationale: The genotype supports imatinib responsiveness, and the anatomy gives shrinkage a consequential operative purpose. The combination supports a neoadjuvant plan rather than treatment from size alone.

answerChoices.label: Primary gastrectomy with margin-negative resection
answerChoices.rationale: Primary surgery treats the local disease but accepts the represented total-gastrectomy extent before exploring genotype-responsive reduction of that morbidity.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: Primary surgery treats the local disease but accepts the represented total-gastrectomy extent before exploring genotype-responsive reduction of that morbidity.

answerChoices.label: Preoperative avapritinib with resection reassessment
answerChoices.rationale: This substitutes a drug associated with another molecular subgroup for an imatinib-responsive KIT exon 11 tumor. Routine preoperative avapritinib is not established here.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: This substitutes a drug associated with another molecular subgroup for an imatinib-responsive KIT exon 11 tumor. Routine preoperative avapritinib is not established here.

questions.explanation: The molecular result and operative cost must both matter. KIT exon 11 supports imatinib responsiveness, while the cardia involvement gives response a reason to precede resection. Reassess the operation after treatment rather than assuming that every large GIST or every kinase inhibitor has the same pathway.

questions.stem: Which systemic-treatment plan best fits {patientName}'s first response assessment for gastric GIST?

exhibit.caption: Original constructed teaching record; fictional patient observations

items.label: Pretreatment tissue and plan
items.value: Core biopsy showed DOG1-positive GIST with a KIT exon 11 deletion. The cardia location prompted preoperative imatinib before the proposed total gastrectomy.

items.label: Matched contrast CT measurements
items.value: The same acquisition phase and lesion region were used. Maximum diameter changed from 8.0 to 10.8 cm; mean attenuation changed from 72 to 34 HU.

items.label: Other imaging observations
items.value: No new enhancing intratumoral nodule or additional lesion is present. There is no internal high-attenuation blood product or peritumoral fluid.

answerChoices.label: Continue the current imatinib regimen
answerChoices.rationale: A substantial fall in attenuation on comparable scans can represent GIST response despite increased size. The lack of a new enhancing nodule or additional lesion supports continuing while the specialist team follows the response, rather than declaring resistance from diameter alone.

answerChoices.label: Escalate the current imatinib regimen
answerChoices.rationale: Size has increased, but the density change is a competing treatment-effect signal. Escalation for presumed resistance should not follow a diameter-only progression call before integrated GIST response review.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: Size has increased, but the density change is a competing treatment-effect signal. Escalation for presumed resistance should not follow a diameter-only progression call before integrated GIST response review.

answerChoices.label: Replace imatinib with sunitinib
answerChoices.rationale: A second-line drug presumes failure or intolerance. The supplied discordant scan does not establish failure, and dose-limiting toxicity is absent.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: A second-line drug presumes failure or intolerance. The supplied discordant scan does not establish failure, and dose-limiting toxicity is absent.

questions.explanation: The larger diameter cannot be ignored, but it cannot be interpreted alone. On matched contrast imaging, the marked attenuation decrease without a new enhancing nodule can reflect imatinib effect even as a GIST enlarges. Continue the current regimen with specialist response review rather than escalate or switch on size alone. This is not a claim that every enlarging low-density lesion is responding.

questions.stem: Which ongoing systemic-treatment plan best fits {patientName}'s gastric-GIST treatment records?

exhibit.caption: Original constructed teaching record; fictional patient observations

items.label: Original disease
items.value: A gastric GIST and biopsy-confirmed liver metastasis both carried a KIT exon 11 alteration.

items.label: Treatment and operation
items.value: Both sites regressed during imatinib. The residual gastric and liver lesions were then completely removed without rupture.

items.label: Current follow-up
items.value: CT shows no visible tumor. She continues imatinib with good tolerance and no progression; she asks about stopping because the scans are clear.

answerChoices.label: Continue imatinib during scan-negative follow-up
answerChoices.rationale: The liver biopsy established metastatic GIST before treatment. Resection and a clear current scan do not convert ongoing effective metastatic therapy into a finite adjuvant course; continue while effective and tolerated.

answerChoices.label: Set an adjuvant-course endpoint and then stop imatinib
answerChoices.rationale: This applies a finite localized-adjuvant framework to previously biopsy-proven metastatic disease. The original liver metastasis remains consequential after all visible sites have been removed.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: This applies a finite localized-adjuvant framework to previously biopsy-proven metastatic disease. The original liver metastasis remains consequential after all visible sites have been removed.

answerChoices.label: Stop imatinib now and restart at measurable recurrence
answerChoices.rationale: A monitored stop-and-restart policy is not equivalent to maintaining effective treatment in metastatic GIST. A current clear scan does not establish that interruption is safe.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: A monitored stop-and-restart policy is not equivalent to maintaining effective treatment in metastatic GIST. A current clear scan does not establish that interruption is safe.

questions.explanation: Interpret the pretreatment liver biopsy before assigning the current treatment phase. This remains previously metastatic GIST despite complete resection and clear scans. Effective, tolerated imatinib continues; neither a finite localized-adjuvant endpoint nor scan-triggered stop-and-restart follows from radiographic clearance.

questions.stem: Which tissue-acquisition plan should be arranged next for {patientName} before choosing treatment for the new gastric-region disease?

exhibit.caption: Original constructed teaching record; fictional patient observations

items.label: History and recent endoscopy
items.value: Gastric MALT lymphoma previously regressed after H. pylori eradication. New forceps samples from the old antral scar show small CD20-positive lymphocytes and lymphoepithelial lesions, without sheets of large cells.

items.label: Interval CT and laboratory results
items.value: A separate posterior gastric/perigastric mass has enlarged from 1.8 to 5.2 cm across the two recent scans. LDH is now 720 U/L (laboratory upper limit 250 U/L); the blood counts are normal.

items.label: PET/CT and endoscopic location map
items.value: The posterior mass has much greater FDG uptake than the old antral scar. It lies outside the mucosal biopsy sites and abuts the posterior gastric wall. No peripheral node is available for sampling.

answerChoices.label: EUS-guided core biopsy of the posterior mass
answerChoices.rationale: The recent small-cell mucosal sample represents the old site, not the rapidly enlarging metabolically discordant mass. Obtain representative tissue from the new lesion to evaluate a changed lymphoma component before selecting treatment; FDG uptake alone does not prove transformation.

answerChoices.label: Repeat forceps biopsies of the antral scar
answerChoices.rationale: The scar biopsy can describe residual MALT at that site but does not classify the separate mass. Repeating the same old-site acquisition leaves the consequential spatial and biologic discrepancy unresolved.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: The scar biopsy can describe residual MALT at that site but does not classify the separate mass. Repeating the same old-site acquisition leaves the consequential spatial and biologic discrepancy unresolved.

answerChoices.label: Iliac-crest marrow aspirate and trephine biopsy
answerChoices.rationale: Marrow assessment may answer selected staging questions, but it does not sample the lesion responsible for the current discrepancy. Normal blood counts do not prove absence of marrow disease; the immediate need is the new mass's histology.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: Marrow assessment may answer selected staging questions, but it does not sample the lesion responsible for the current discrepancy. Normal blood counts do not prove absence of marrow disease; the immediate need is the new mass's histology.

questions.explanation: A low-grade result from the old mucosal scar cannot classify a different rapidly enlarging, more FDG-avid mass. The clinical and imaging discrepancy raises concern for a changed component, but requires histologic confirmation. Use the PET/location map to obtain representative tissue from that mass rather than repeat the old scar or substitute a staging specimen.

questions.stem: Which initial systemic regimen best fits {patientName}'s gastric diffuse large-B-cell lymphoma and pretreatment findings among the options offered?

exhibit.caption: Original constructed teaching record; fictional patient observations

items.label: Lymphoma record
items.value: Gastric biopsies establish CD20-positive diffuse large-B-cell lymphoma. Systemic treatment with curative intent is planned. There is no perforation, ongoing hemorrhage or obstruction.

items.label: Functional assessment
items.value: She is independently active, walks without assistance and has preserved renal and hepatic function. There is no general frailty limiting combination treatment.

items.label: Cardiac assessment
items.value: Longstanding ischemic cardiomyopathy predates the lymphoma. Repeat echocardiography after cardiac optimization shows left ventricular ejection fraction 30%; previous examinations show similar values.

answerChoices.label: R-CEOP combination immunochemotherapy
answerChoices.rationale: Persistent marked systolic dysfunction makes doxorubicin exposure the limiting issue despite preserved general function. R-CEOP substitutes etoposide for doxorubicin and is a guideline-supported offered option for anthracycline-ineligible large-B-cell lymphoma, with hematology and cardio-oncology review.

answerChoices.label: R-CHOP combination immunochemotherapy
answerChoices.rationale: R-CHOP includes doxorubicin. Otherwise good function does not remove the persistent severe systolic dysfunction that changes the appropriate drug backbone.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: R-CHOP includes doxorubicin. Otherwise good function does not remove the persistent severe systolic dysfunction that changes the appropriate drug backbone.

answerChoices.label: R-mini-CHOP combination immunochemotherapy
answerChoices.rationale: Dose-attenuated R-mini-CHOP retains doxorubicin; it does not remove the drug constrained by this cardiac assessment. The record supports a cardiac-specific substitution rather than treating an independently active 69-year-old as generally frail.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: Dose-attenuated R-mini-CHOP retains doxorubicin; it does not remove the drug constrained by this cardiac assessment. The record supports a cardiac-specific substitution rather than treating an independently active 69-year-old as generally frail.

questions.explanation: The biopsy establishes the lymphoma family, but the regimen comparison turns on pretreatment fitness. Persistent severe systolic dysfunction changes whether doxorubicin belongs in the regimen; preserved independence does not cancel that constraint. R-CEOP is the supported offered anthracycline-free alternative. Simply reducing CHOP doses still exposes her to doxorubicin. Other specialist alternatives exist; this item does not rank them or prescribe doses or cycles.

decisionNodes.stem: Which next tissue-acquisition procedure best fits {patientName}'s gastric-wall findings and the need for tumor classification and sequencing?

answerChoices.label: EUS-guided core biopsy of the solid component
answerChoices.rationale: The submitted mucosa does not represent the fourth-layer mass. EUS can target its solid component through the adjacent gastric wall and obtain tissue for classification and molecular testing without committing to a reconstructive resection.

answerChoices.label: CT-guided core biopsy of the solid component
answerChoices.rationale: Percutaneous core biopsy is a legitimate alternative for some GISTs, but the represented direct trajectory crosses colon while the solid target borders the gastric lumen. This anatomy favors EUS; percutaneous biopsy is not categorically prohibited.

answerChoices.label: Laparoscopic wedge excision of the wall mass
answerChoices.rationale: Excision would obtain diagnostic tissue but here entails gastroesophageal-junction reconstruction before the tumor type is known. Representative needle tissue can determine whether such an operation is appropriate.

decisionNodes.explanation: The benign mucosal sample and the fourth-layer mass describe different compartments. After recognizing that mismatch, compare routes to solid tumor rather than repeat superficial sampling or use a cystic component. The represented luminal relationship, transcolonic percutaneous trajectory and reconstructive cost of excision favor EUS-guided core tissue. Archived tissue from a different specimen must not substitute merely because a report is attached to the referral.

After recognizing that mismatch, compare routes to solid tumor rather than repeat superficial sampling or use a cystic component. Archived tissue from a different specimen must not substitute merely because a report is attached to the referral.

decisionNodes.stem: Which initial tumor-treatment plan best fits {patientName}'s gastric-mass records?

answerChoices.label: Preoperative imatinib with resection reassessment
answerChoices.rationale: The genotype supports imatinib responsiveness, and the anatomy gives shrinkage a consequential operative purpose. The combination supports a neoadjuvant plan rather than treatment from size alone.

answerChoices.label: Primary gastrectomy with margin-negative resection
answerChoices.rationale: Primary surgery treats the local disease but accepts the represented total-gastrectomy extent before exploring genotype-responsive reduction of that morbidity.

answerChoices.label: Preoperative avapritinib with resection reassessment
answerChoices.rationale: This substitutes a drug associated with another molecular subgroup for an imatinib-responsive KIT exon 11 tumor. Routine preoperative avapritinib is not established here.

decisionNodes.explanation: The molecular result and operative cost must both matter. KIT exon 11 supports imatinib responsiveness, while the cardia involvement gives response a reason to precede resection. Reassess the operation after treatment rather than assuming that every large GIST or every kinase inhibitor has the same pathway.

decisionNodes.stem: Which systemic-treatment plan best fits {patientName}'s first response assessment for gastric GIST?

answerChoices.label: Continue the current imatinib regimen
answerChoices.rationale: A substantial fall in attenuation on comparable scans can represent GIST response despite increased size. The lack of a new enhancing nodule or additional lesion supports continuing while the specialist team follows the response, rather than declaring resistance from diameter alone.

answerChoices.label: Escalate the current imatinib regimen
answerChoices.rationale: Size has increased, but the density change is a competing treatment-effect signal. Escalation for presumed resistance should not follow a diameter-only progression call before integrated GIST response review.

answerChoices.label: Replace imatinib with sunitinib
answerChoices.rationale: A second-line drug presumes failure or intolerance. The supplied discordant scan does not establish failure, and dose-limiting toxicity is absent.

decisionNodes.explanation: The larger diameter cannot be ignored, but it cannot be interpreted alone. On matched contrast imaging, the marked attenuation decrease without a new enhancing nodule can reflect imatinib effect even as a GIST enlarges. Continue the current regimen with specialist response review rather than escalate or switch on size alone. This is not a claim that every enlarging low-density lesion is responding.

items.label: Pretreatment tissue and plan
items.value: Core biopsy showed DOG1-positive GIST with a KIT exon 11 deletion. The cardia location prompted preoperative imatinib before the proposed total gastrectomy.

items.label: Matched contrast CT measurements
items.value: The same acquisition phase and lesion region were used. Maximum diameter changed from 8.0 to 10.8 cm; mean attenuation changed from 72 to 34 HU.

items.label: Other imaging observations
items.value: No new enhancing intratumoral nodule or additional lesion is present. There is no internal high-attenuation blood product or peritumoral fluid.

decisionNodes.stem: Which ongoing systemic-treatment plan best fits {patientName}'s gastric-GIST treatment records?

answerChoices.label: Continue imatinib during scan-negative follow-up
answerChoices.rationale: The liver biopsy established metastatic GIST before treatment. Resection and a clear current scan do not convert ongoing effective metastatic therapy into a finite adjuvant course; continue while effective and tolerated.

answerChoices.label: Set an adjuvant-course endpoint and then stop imatinib
answerChoices.rationale: This applies a finite localized-adjuvant framework to previously biopsy-proven metastatic disease. The original liver metastasis remains consequential after all visible sites have been removed.

answerChoices.label: Stop imatinib now and restart at measurable recurrence
answerChoices.rationale: A monitored stop-and-restart policy is not equivalent to maintaining effective treatment in metastatic GIST. A current clear scan does not establish that interruption is safe.

decisionNodes.explanation: Interpret the pretreatment liver biopsy before assigning the current treatment phase. This remains previously metastatic GIST despite complete resection and clear scans. Effective, tolerated imatinib continues; neither a finite localized-adjuvant endpoint nor scan-triggered stop-and-restart follows from radiographic clearance.

exhibit.caption: Original constructed teaching record; fictional patient observations

items.label: Original disease
items.value: A gastric GIST and biopsy-confirmed liver metastasis both carried a KIT exon 11 alteration.

items.label: Treatment and operation
items.value: Both sites regressed during imatinib. The residual gastric and liver lesions were then completely removed without rupture.

items.label: Current follow-up
items.value: CT shows no visible tumor. She continues imatinib with good tolerance and no progression; she asks about stopping because the scans are clear.

decisionNodes.stem: Which tissue-acquisition plan should be arranged next for {patientName} before choosing treatment for the new gastric-region disease?

answerChoices.label: EUS-guided core biopsy of the posterior mass
answerChoices.rationale: The recent small-cell mucosal sample represents the old site, not the rapidly enlarging metabolically discordant mass. Obtain representative tissue from the new lesion to evaluate a changed lymphoma component before selecting treatment; FDG uptake alone does not prove transformation.

answerChoices.label: Repeat forceps biopsies of the antral scar
answerChoices.rationale: The scar biopsy can describe residual MALT at that site but does not classify the separate mass. Repeating the same old-site acquisition leaves the consequential spatial and biologic discrepancy unresolved.

answerChoices.label: Iliac-crest marrow aspirate and trephine biopsy
answerChoices.rationale: Marrow assessment may answer selected staging questions, but it does not sample the lesion responsible for the current discrepancy. Normal blood counts do not prove absence of marrow disease; the immediate need is the new mass's histology.

decisionNodes.explanation: A low-grade result from the old mucosal scar cannot classify a different rapidly enlarging, more FDG-avid mass. The clinical and imaging discrepancy raises concern for a changed component, but requires histologic confirmation. Use the PET/location map to obtain representative tissue from that mass rather than repeat the old scar or substitute a staging specimen.

exhibit.caption: Original constructed teaching record; fictional patient observations

items.label: History and recent endoscopy
items.value: Gastric MALT lymphoma previously regressed after H. pylori eradication. New forceps samples from the old antral scar show small CD20-positive lymphocytes and lymphoepithelial lesions, without sheets of large cells.

items.label: Interval CT and laboratory results
items.value: A separate posterior gastric/perigastric mass has enlarged from 1.8 to 5.2 cm across the two recent scans. LDH is now 720 U/L (laboratory upper limit 250 U/L); the blood counts are normal.

items.label: PET/CT and endoscopic location map
items.value: The posterior mass has much greater FDG uptake than the old antral scar. It lies outside the mucosal biopsy sites and abuts the posterior gastric wall. No peripheral node is available for sampling.

decisionNodes.currentUpdate: The clinic reviews outside hematopathology and pretreatment assessment for a hematology planning visit.
decisionNodes.stem: Which initial systemic regimen best fits {patientName}'s gastric diffuse large-B-cell lymphoma and pretreatment findings among the options offered?

answerChoices.label: R-CEOP combination immunochemotherapy
answerChoices.rationale: Persistent marked systolic dysfunction makes doxorubicin exposure the limiting issue despite preserved general function. R-CEOP substitutes etoposide for doxorubicin and is a guideline-supported offered option for anthracycline-ineligible large-B-cell lymphoma, with hematology and cardio-oncology review.

answerChoices.label: R-CHOP combination immunochemotherapy
answerChoices.rationale: R-CHOP includes doxorubicin. Otherwise good function does not remove the persistent severe systolic dysfunction that changes the appropriate drug backbone.

answerChoices.label: R-mini-CHOP combination immunochemotherapy
answerChoices.rationale: Dose-attenuated R-mini-CHOP retains doxorubicin; it does not remove the drug constrained by this cardiac assessment. The record supports a cardiac-specific substitution rather than treating an independently active 69-year-old as generally frail.

decisionNodes.explanation: The biopsy establishes the lymphoma family, but the regimen comparison turns on pretreatment fitness. Persistent severe systolic dysfunction changes whether doxorubicin belongs in the regimen; preserved independence does not cancel that constraint. R-CEOP is the supported offered anthracycline-free alternative. Simply reducing CHOP doses still exposes her to doxorubicin. Other specialist alternatives exist; this item does not rank them or prescribe doses or cycles.

exhibit.caption: Original constructed teaching record; fictional patient observations

items.label: Lymphoma record
items.value: Gastric biopsies establish CD20-positive diffuse large-B-cell lymphoma. Systemic treatment with curative intent is planned. There is no perforation, ongoing hemorrhage or obstruction.

items.label: Functional assessment
items.value: She is independently active, walks without assistance and has preserved renal and hepatic function. There is no general frailty limiting combination treatment.

items.label: Cardiac assessment
items.value: Longstanding ischemic cardiomyopathy predates the lymphoma. Repeat echocardiography after cardiac optimization shows left ventricular ejection fraction 30%; previous examinations show similar values.

manualAuthorChecks.coverTheKey: No report declares the sample inadequate or the lesion reachable. Raw specimen layers and route geometry must be compared with the target before choosing among three tissue procedures.
manualAuthorChecks.sameDecisionStageAndCategory: All choices obtain representative tumor tissue now; none is a repeated unchanged forceps biopsy or an unrelated staging test.
reasoningSteps: Infer that glands and lamina propria do not classify a fourth-layer mass even though the surface biopsy is benign.
Compare access to solid tumor and the cost of diagnostic excision; choose EUS core in this represented anatomy.
manualAuthorChecks.closestError: CT-guided core is a credible technique but ignores the colon on the represented skin-to-solid-target trajectory.
manualAuthorChecks.decidingObservation: Solid tumor borders the luminal wall, while colon lies on the direct percutaneous trajectory and a wedge crosses the gastroesophageal junction.
manualAuthorChecks.consequence: Obtain classifying and sequenceable tumor tissue without an avoidable transcolonic approach or reconstructive diagnostic excision.
manualAuthorChecks.residentDifficulty: Moderate after repair: compartment interpretation followed by access selection; not labeled hard merely because EUS is specialized.
manualAuthorChecks.singleDefensibleBestAnswer: EUS core is the best offered route for these observations. No universal EUS-over-percutaneous rule or invented assay-adequacy threshold is asserted.
manualAuthorChecks.counterfactual: With solid tumor beyond EUS reach and a safe skin trajectory, CT-guided core could become the preferred offered procedure.
deletionTest: Delete the specimen layers and the reason a benign report fails to classify the mass is lost.
Delete route geometry and the EUS-versus-percutaneous preference is less discriminating; no prediction of treatment benefit is supplied.
manualAuthorChecks.sequenceReview: Self-contained singleton; no prior explanation announces preoperative imatinib and no later genotype is exposed.
manualAuthorChecks.repairAndRecheck: One review response removed feasibility language and the weak unchanged-forceps foil, retained neutral anatomy, and incorporated provenance as unscored feedback. Re-review remains required.

manualAuthorChecks.coverTheKey: The record gives cardia encirclement and the proposed operation without predicting shrinkage, organ preservation or a preferred treatment sequence. Genotype and operative morbidity must both inform the plan.
manualAuthorChecks.sameDecisionStageAndCategory: Three initial local-tumor treatment strategies.
reasoningSteps: Interpret the diagnostic phenotype and KIT exon 11 deletion as an imatinib-responsive GIST.
Use the cardia-related total-gastrectomy consequence to favor preoperative response before resection.
manualAuthorChecks.closestError: Proceed to total gastrectomy because the disease is localized and technically removable.
manualAuthorChecks.decidingObservation: KIT exon 11 supplies drug sensitivity; cardia encirclement with proposed total gastrectomy supplies a consequential reason to consider treatment before surgery.
manualAuthorChecks.consequence: The wrong sequence can impose avoidable gastric loss or expose the patient to an unsuitable drug.
manualAuthorChecks.residentDifficulty: Moderate to hard PGY-2/3 prediction from genotype versus operability, not the source's former sensitivity label.
manualAuthorChecks.singleDefensibleBestAnswer: Among these options, preoperative imatinib addresses both a responsive driver and the represented avoidable surgical extent.
manualAuthorChecks.counterfactual: Change cardia encirclement to a peripheral wedge-resectable lesion: primary surgery becomes preferable. Change to metastatic D842V: avapritinib becomes the appropriate offered drug in that revised indication.
deletionTest: Without genotype, imatinib responsiveness is not established and empiric treatment is unsafe.
Without the morbid operative anatomy, a readily resectable localized GIST could favor primary surgery; size alone does not dictate neoadjuvant therapy.
manualAuthorChecks.sequenceReview: Self-contained singleton repeats pathology and extent; the prior tissue-acquisition item and its treatment-scaffolding feedback are absent.
manualAuthorChecks.repairAndRecheck: One review response removed the explicit organ-preservation prediction and split the returned chain. The already defensible genotype-by-anatomy decision remains; independent re-review is pending.

manualAuthorChecks.coverTheKey: Neither improved symptoms nor a qualitative radiology response conclusion is supplied. A large diameter increase competes with the raw matched-protocol attenuation decrease.
manualAuthorChecks.sameDecisionStageAndCategory: Three current systemic-treatment plans compare continuation, dose escalation and line change after the same first response assessment.
reasoningSteps: Interpret increased diameter together with lower attenuation and absence of new enhancing tumor on comparable scans.
Distinguish possible targeted-treatment response from established failure before deciding whether to continue or change treatment.
manualAuthorChecks.closestError: Escalating imatinib after reading only the increased diameter is the nearest credible error; the size change is no longer a small subthreshold distraction.

manualAuthorChecks.consequence: Avoid prematurely abandoning or escalating effective treatment on a size-only progression interpretation.

manualAuthorChecks.counterfactual: A new enhancing intratumoral nodule or additional progressive sites would defeat the simple response interpretation and prompt resistance evaluation.
deletionTest: Hide attenuation and the large diameter increase makes progression and escalation credible; density is necessary to the scored choice.

reasoningSteps: Reconcile current radiographic clearance with the original biopsy-proven metastatic distribution.
Apply metastatic suppression rather than localized-adjuvant completion logic to the ongoing drug plan.
manualAuthorChecks.closestError: Applying a finite adjuvant endpoint after complete metastasectomy is the nearest error, distinct from stopping immediately because the present scan is clear.
manualAuthorChecks.decidingObservation: The original liver lesion was biopsy-confirmed metastatic GIST and the same drug remains effective and tolerated.
manualAuthorChecks.consequence: Routine interruption can permit progression despite apparent remission.
manualAuthorChecks.residentDifficulty: Moderate to hard PGY-2/3 prediction from treatment-intent and current-versus-historical disease-state confusion.
manualAuthorChecks.singleDefensibleBestAnswer: Continue imatinib among the offered choices because the disease was metastatic and neither failure nor intolerance justifies changing therapy.
manualAuthorChecks.counterfactual: Without an original metastatic site, completely resected localized high-risk sensitive GIST could warrant a finite adjuvant course; intolerance would require a different reassessment rather than a clearance-based stop.
deletionTest: Original metastatic tissue provenance prevents a benign liver lesion from being misread as spread.
Resection and clear CT make stopping genuinely tempting.
Current response and tolerance distinguish a continuation decision from drug failure management.
manualAuthorChecks.sequenceReview: Self-contained singleton preserves original biopsy-proven metastasis, operative clearance and tolerability; no prerequisite case supplies its disease-phase conclusion.
manualAuthorChecks.repairAndRecheck: One response neutralized the task and replaced the disposable sunitinib foil with a finite-adjuvant policy. No arbitrary stopping interval or new duration rule was introduced; re-review is pending.

manualAuthorChecks.sameDecisionStageAndCategory: All three options are specific tissue-acquisition plans before treatment selection; no drug or unrelated local staging procedure is a category outlier.
reasoningSteps: Interpret discordant growth, LDH and FDG avidity despite small-cell histology from a different gastric site as an unresolved possible changed component.
Choose tissue from the changing mass rather than repeat a nonrepresentative old site or substitute marrow staging.

manualAuthorChecks.decidingObservation: The rapidly enlarging FDG-avid posterior mass lies outside the antral mucosal biopsy sites; no specimen yet classifies that mass.
manualAuthorChecks.consequence: Avoid selecting a low-grade or aggressive treatment pathway without representative confirmation of the new lesion.
