assertions.text: Select representative pretreatment tissue and molecular evaluation for a challenging gastric-wall mass.

The benign mucosal sample and the fourth-layer mass describe different compartments. After recognizing that mismatch, compare routes to solid tumor rather than repeat superficial sampling or use a cystic component. The represented luminal relationship, transcolonic percutaneous trajectory and reconstructive cost of excision favor EUS-guided core tissue. Archived tissue from a different specimen must not substitute merely because a report is attached to the referral.

The submitted mucosa does not represent the fourth-layer mass. EUS can target its solid component through the adjacent gastric wall and obtain tissue for classification and molecular testing without committing to a reconstructive resection.
An extraluminal solid target inaccessible to EUS with a safe percutaneous trajectory would favor an image-guided percutaneous core instead.

Percutaneous core biopsy is a legitimate alternative for some GISTs, but the represented direct trajectory crosses colon while the solid target borders the gastric lumen. This anatomy favors EUS; percutaneous biopsy is not categorically prohibited.
A safely accessible extraluminal target beyond EUS reach would make a percutaneous core a reasonable choice.

Excision would obtain diagnostic tissue but here entails gastroesophageal-junction reconstruction before the tumor type is known. Representative needle tissue can determine whether such an operation is appropriate.
A small readily resectable lesion, or a symptomatic lesion that cannot be sampled safely, may reasonably undergo excision in a specialist pathway.

statementMappings.constructedBasis: Original fictional measurements, anatomy and chronology; not empirical cutoffs, medication doses, probabilities or waiting durations.

assertions.text: Apply GIST genotype and cardia anatomy to the choice of preoperative targeted treatment.

The molecular result and operative cost must both matter. KIT exon 11 supports imatinib responsiveness, while the cardia involvement gives response a reason to precede resection. Reassess the operation after treatment rather than assuming that every large GIST or every kinase inhibitor has the same pathway.
The genotype supports imatinib responsiveness, and the anatomy gives shrinkage a consequential operative purpose. The combination supports a neoadjuvant plan rather than treatment from size alone.
A similarly genotyped peripheral lesion removable by a small wedge would favor primary surgery rather than automatically adding preoperative treatment.
Primary surgery treats the local disease but accepts the represented total-gastrectomy extent before exploring genotype-responsive reduction of that morbidity.
A straightforward limited resection, an urgent complication or an imatinib-resistant genotype can change the initial plan.
This substitutes a drug associated with another molecular subgroup for an imatinib-responsive KIT exon 11 tumor. Routine preoperative avapritinib is not established here.
PDGFRA D842V with unresectable or metastatic disease supports avapritinib; that is a different genotype and indication.

statementMappings.constructedBasis: Original fictional measurements, anatomy and chronology; not empirical cutoffs, medication doses, probabilities or waiting durations.

assertions.text: Interpret paired CT size and attenuation changes before declaring imatinib failure in gastric GIST.

The larger diameter cannot be ignored, but it cannot be interpreted alone. On matched contrast imaging, the marked attenuation decrease without a new enhancing nodule can reflect imatinib effect even as a GIST enlarges. Continue the current regimen with specialist response review rather than escalate or switch on size alone. This is not a claim that every enlarging low-density lesion is responding.

A substantial fall in attenuation on comparable scans can represent GIST response despite increased size. The lack of a new enhancing nodule or additional lesion supports continuing while the specialist team follows the response, rather than declaring resistance from diameter alone.
New enhancing viable tumor or additional progressive sites would require reassessment for true progression rather than continuation on the basis of low mean density alone.

Size has increased, but the density change is a competing treatment-effect signal. Escalation for presumed resistance should not follow a diameter-only progression call before integrated GIST response review.
Confirmed progression after adherence, interactions and imaging have been reviewed can make dose escalation a specialist option in appropriate disease.
A second-line drug presumes failure or intolerance. The supplied discordant scan does not establish failure, and dose-limiting toxicity is absent.
Confirmed imatinib resistance or relevant intolerance would make second-line treatment a different decision.

statementMappings.constructedBasis: Original fictional measurements, anatomy and chronology; not empirical cutoffs, medication doses, probabilities or waiting durations.

assertions.text: Maintain effective imatinib after response and removal of metastatic gastric GIST rather than apply a finite-adjuvant stopping rule.

Interpret the pretreatment liver biopsy before assigning the current treatment phase. This remains previously metastatic GIST despite complete resection and clear scans. Effective, tolerated imatinib continues; neither a finite localized-adjuvant endpoint nor scan-triggered stop-and-restart follows from radiographic clearance.

The liver biopsy established metastatic GIST before treatment. Resection and a clear current scan do not convert ongoing effective metastatic therapy into a finite adjuvant course; continue while effective and tolerated.
A completely resected localized primary without metastasis would instead raise a risk- and genotype-dependent finite adjuvant decision.
This applies a finite localized-adjuvant framework to previously biopsy-proven metastatic disease. The original liver metastasis remains consequential after all visible sites have been removed.
If the original disease had been confined to a completely resected primary, a finite evidence-supported adjuvant course could be appropriate for a sensitive high-risk tumor.
A monitored stop-and-restart policy is not equivalent to maintaining effective treatment in metastatic GIST. A current clear scan does not establish that interruption is safe.
Relevant intolerance would require a toxicity-driven treatment reassessment; it is absent here and is not a scan-clearance stopping rule.

assertions.text: Select a representative biopsy site when a new gastric-region lesion behaves differently from previously sampled MALT lymphoma.

A low-grade result from the old mucosal scar cannot classify a different rapidly enlarging, more FDG-avid mass. The clinical and imaging discrepancy raises concern for a changed component, but requires histologic confirmation. Use the PET/location map to obtain representative tissue from that mass rather than repeat the old scar or substitute a staging specimen.

The recent small-cell mucosal sample represents the old site, not the rapidly enlarging metabolically discordant mass. Obtain representative tissue from the new lesion to evaluate a changed lymphoma component before selecting treatment; FDG uptake alone does not prove transformation.
If representative tissue from the changing mass had already established its histology, repeating acquisition would not answer a remaining staging question.

The scar biopsy can describe residual MALT at that site but does not classify the separate mass. Repeating the same old-site acquisition leaves the consequential spatial and biologic discrepancy unresolved.
If the uncertain progressive lesion were mucosal and located in that scar, directed repeat endoscopic sampling could be representative.

Marrow assessment may answer selected staging questions, but it does not sample the lesion responsible for the current discrepancy. Normal blood counts do not prove absence of marrow disease; the immediate need is the new mass's histology.
A specific marrow or cytopenia question could justify marrow sampling, but would not replace biopsy of a discordant mass suspected of a changed component.

assertions.text: Distinguish an anthracycline-free lymphoma regimen from simple dose attenuation when cardiac dysfunction constrains treatment of gastric large-B-cell lymphoma.

The biopsy establishes the lymphoma family, but the regimen comparison turns on pretreatment fitness. Persistent severe systolic dysfunction changes whether doxorubicin belongs in the regimen; preserved independence does not cancel that constraint. R-CEOP is the supported offered anthracycline-free alternative. Simply reducing CHOP doses still exposes her to doxorubicin. Other specialist alternatives exist; this item does not rank them or prescribe doses or cycles.

Persistent marked systolic dysfunction makes doxorubicin exposure the limiting issue despite preserved general function. R-CEOP substitutes etoposide for doxorubicin and is a guideline-supported offered option for anthracycline-ineligible large-B-cell lymphoma, with hematology and cardio-oncology review.
With preserved cardiac function and no anthracycline contraindication, an anthracycline-containing first-line regimen could be preferred; R-CEOP is not claimed superior for all patients.
R-CHOP includes doxorubicin. Otherwise good function does not remove the persistent severe systolic dysfunction that changes the appropriate drug backbone.
Preserved systolic function without a relevant anthracycline contraindication would make R-CHOP a defensible first-line option in an appropriate disease setting.

Dose-attenuated R-mini-CHOP retains doxorubicin; it does not remove the drug constrained by this cardiac assessment. The record supports a cardiac-specific substitution rather than treating an independently active 69-year-old as generally frail.
A suitable very elderly patient without this cardiac constraint may be considered for attenuated R-mini-CHOP; that different fitness problem is not represented here.
